speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The object of the Bill is to provide for an inspection of these companies, there being none at present. There is a provision in the existing Act under which the Minister of Finance may, if he so desires, have an inspection made of any particular company. He is not in a position, however, to know what companies should or should not be inspected; and complaints are not made about companies until something is wrong with them, when inspection is generally too late. Trust and loan companies' will both be made subject to inspection because I shall introduce in a moment another Bill dealing with the latter class. The new legislation will place
both trust and loan companies in exactly the same position as insurance companies. An annual inspection is provided for because only by an annual inspection is it possible for any one to tell when special examinations ought to be made.

I regret to have to again call the attention of the House to a most important and urgent question, I refer to the ice jam on the St. Lawrence river. On the 9th of March I drew the attention of the Minister of Marine to the condition in question; stating that I had been informed from reliable sources that there was imminent danger of floods. The minister then answered to the following effect:
X am afraid that the information that has reached the hon. member is not accurate.* * * With no ice bridge formed at this point, there is no fear of disastrous floods occurring above. The channel is now clear of ice up to a point near Portneuf. 35 miles above Quebec, where the Lady Grey is working to-day, and is making good progress.
j do not anticipate any serious results from floods this spring-no one can accurately tell-but I am pleased to say that the Lady Grey is working so well and that the ice bridge is broken.

I have no doubt that the minister was sincere and in earnest in his statement but I believe he has been wrongly informed. In the Montreal Gazette of Friday, March 26 it is stated that at Three Rivers the ice barrage is still solid and trouble is feared as the water continues to rise gradually in the St. Lawrence. It is also reported that the ice barrage at Three Rivers is still solid clear across to the South shore, and that the Lady Grey will not be able to break through the ice that blocks the river for miles above this point.
In the reports of the Press yesterday-

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the
hon. member for Chambly-Vereheres (Mr. Archambault) I. cannot to-day give him information very much different from that which I furnished him a few days ago. The continued disturbance in Germany, more particularly in Berlin, as a result of the revolutions and counter revolutions, have a decidedly local interest to Stratford, inasmuch as Captain John A. Barron, R.A.F., son of His Honour Judge Barron, is now and has been for some weeks at Berlin, the chief centre of the disturbances. As one of the entente officers selected by the allies to adjust certain claims upon the Germans, in relation to Zeppelins and airships, he was required to meet with German officers, and it is seen by the press that the reception by the latter was far from cordial, in fact at times it assumed the shape of aggressive force, and one at least of the French officers had died as the result of these attacks, and others have been injured. For some time Captain Barron has not been heard from by his friends in Ottawa.
I would like to ask the Government two questions:	(1) Has the Government any

On the Orders of the Day:
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council):	The hon. member
for Quebec South (Mr. Power) inquired on Thursday last as to the accuracy of the rumour that the district Pension Office at Quebec,and at certain other cities had been or were about to be closed, and I promised to secure information on the subject. I am now advised by the Chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners that the board has decided to close the district Pension
m\r\rnvs
Office at Quebec and some fourteen other district offices throughout Canada. The statement by the Chairman of the board is as follows:
District Offices were originally opened for the purpose of investigating applications for pensions made 'by dependent parents. There was no thought in the beginning of performing any medical work in connection with the District Offices. The medical work was all performed by military Medical Boards. After the armistice the cases of dependent parents for investigations immediately became very few in number but the medical work in connection with de^ mobilization became very heavy. The medical work was, therefore, taken out of the hands of the military Medical Boards and doctors were sent from head office to each of the district offices to make medical re-examinations, etc. At the present time a district office exists mainly to re-examine disability cases from time to time.
About eight months ago it was realized that District Offices would eventually have to be closed and in order to make this possible a scheme of travelling Medical Boards was originated to re-examine pensioners in all centres where a number could be brought together at a particular time, that is to say in towns of a population of two thousand or more. This travelling medical board scheme is now in operation in the Eastern Provinces and is ready to be put into operation in the Western Provinces. The result is that pensioners attached to the Charlottetown and Sydney District Offices are being re-examined by travelling Medical Boards from Halifax; those attached to Quebec by travelling Medical Boards from Montreal; those attached to Kingston and North Bay by travelling Medical Boards from Toronto ; those attached to Windsor by travelling (Medical Boards from London and those attached to Port Arthur by travelling Medical Boards from Winnipeg. Travelling Medical Boards will also, in the near future, deal with pensioners attached to Regina, Saskatoon, Victoria, St. John and possibly Hamilton. As soon as these travelling Medical Boards have been in operation for a month or two the necessity for keeping offices open in all the smaller cities will no longer exist.
At the present time there are twenty-one District Offices which cost this commission an average of over one hundred thousand dollars a month, that is to say more than two-thirds the total cost of administration. Of course the smaller District Offices cost this commission proportionately less in accordance with their size but the closing of each of these offices will result in a saving of not less than five thousand dollars a year for the smallest District Office, namely Charlottetown, and not less than thirty thousand dollars a year for some of the medium-sized District Offices which it is proposed to close.
It is estimated that the closing of offices which can now be dispensed with will mean an annual saving of between $400,000 and $500,000 in the administration of the Pensions Board.	,
With reference particularly to the Quebec District Office, this office has, from the time it was opened, has been extraordinarily expensive when its size is considered. There are less than one thousand pensioners resident in the Quebec district which takes in the north shore of the 
St. Lawrence from Three Rivers and the south shore from Levis east. The office has been reorganized on two occasions but is still the most expensive of this commission when its size is considered. For the eleven months just past the expenditure in connection with this office has been about $23,000. By closing the office and doing the re-examinations of pensioners by the travelling Medical Board from Montreal it is thought that at least three-quarters of this expenditure can be saved and the service to the pensioner will be quite as good.
The same thing, although perhaps to not as great an extent, can be said with regard to the District Offices which it is proposed to close.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the statement of the Chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners as to the action which the Board has taken and is about to take and the reasons therefor. The Board is convinced that by adopting this course efficient service can be given to the pensioners and at the same time the very large sum mentioned can be, saved annually to the country. Members of the House know that the Board is constituted by statute and that its members are carrying out their duties under that statute.

speechtext:
When we are in
Supply, I shall not ask the committee to take up Civil Government to-day, but I shall be pleased to take up some Estimates other than Civil Government.
Air. Speaker, when the House resolves itself into Committee of Supply to-day, it is my intention to take up the Railways and Canals Estimates. It has been the custom to present an annual statement as to the operation of the Canadian Government railways. In presenting the Estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals for the forthcoming fiscal year, I desire to place before the House a statement dealing with the operation of the Canadian National Railways for the calendar year 1919. The Canadian Northern was merged with the Government railways in December, 1918, so that we are now in a position to review one completed year of operation under nonpolitical and purely business auspices. The
8G0

National system, with which we are now dealing, comprises the following lines:'-
Miles.
Canadian Northern railway system 9,479
Intercolonial	 1,592
Prince Edward Island	[DOT]	..	278
National Transcontinental	2,002
Branch lines	 376
Total	13,727
It is unfortunate that abnormal economic conditions, the disturbing effects of which are world-wide and beyond the control of any railroad management, whether public or private, should have prevented a better showing for the first year of large scale national operation, but the result, when .closely analysed, is not without hope for the future of Government ownership and operation.
More Revenue but Greater Operating Costs.
Briefly stated, the National system comprising
The Canadian Northern,
The Intercolonial, and The Transcontinental,
earned $94,000,000 during the year, or almost $12,000,000 more than during 1918. But even with the $12,000,000 increased earnings, the operating' loss is $14,000,000, made up as follows:
Canadian Northern	$6,500,000
Intercolonial and Transcontinental	 7,500,000

The explanation of this is that during the year the operating expenses advanced from 84 to practically 108 millions, an adverse increase of nearly 24 millions. For the most part, this was due to advances in wages under the McAdoo award and supplements thereto, which were not offset by corresponding increases in rates. There was no rate increase during 1919. Given the same operating costs as 1918, the earnings for 1919 would have taken care of them and provided in addition the tidy sum of nine millions towards meeting fixed charges. These interest obligations in themselves amount to nineteen millions, and, singularly enough, a comparison of the payroll of the National system for the two years shows an increase of practically nineteen millions in wages alone during 1919.
The operating loss of fourteen millions, and the consequent failure to provide for fixed charges, is really a reflection of conditions which obtain all over the world as a result of the war. Comparisons are seldom

conclusive, but sometimes they are illuminating, and in passing, I am reminded that in the United States, where economic con- ' ditions so closely approximate our own. the lines taken over by the Government for operation during the war are reported to have failed in two years by over seven hundred millions to earn the net revenue which the Government guaranteed them when taken over by the United States Railroad Administration.
More Passengers but Less Freight.
Although the freight earnings of the National system show an increase in excess of two and a half millions for the year, there was a falling off in freight handled amounting to three million tons. This was due in part to the stoppage of munition shipments on cessation of hostilities, and four-fifths of the decreased tonnage was on the old Canadian Government system, which formerly handled so much war business. There was a noticeable falling off also in -westbound business, due to unsettled conditions in the period of transition from war to peace. That there was an increase in freight earnings at all is attributable to the increased rates put into effect during 1918, to which 1 shall refer more fully later on. Had the volume of freight handled during the preceding year been maintained, the increased freight earnings would have amounted to seven and a half millions instead of two and a half. Thus the return of the world to a peace basis may be said to have cost the National system five millions in freight revenue during the year 1919. But no one will say it was not worth while.
The National system carried eleven and a half million passengers during the year, an increase of about one and three quarter millions. Additional services and the return troop movement helped to swell these figures. Total passenger earnings increased from fourteen to a little less than twenty-two million dollars. About a million and a half of this increased revenue is attributable to the 10 per cent increase in passenger rates granted during 1918, and in effect for the first time for the full year. The coupling up of the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Government railways has, I may say, resulted in an increase in better paying long-haul business, and the management has every expectation that this business will be maintained, notwithstanding the completion of troop movements.
Operating Costs.	[DOT]
I shall try not to weary the House with an endless procession of figures, but as

*briefly as possible call attention to their significance, and then append to this verbal .statement detailed statistical information, which, with the permission of hon. members, could appear as appendices to these remarks, and thus receive the leisured scrutiny which their importance warrants. The tables to which I refer differentiate between Canadian National and former Canadian Government lines, and, as well, give the totals for the entire system, with which I have been dealing. They do not, however, include the Grand Trunk Pacific, which, pending the taking over of the Grand Trunk system, has been operated as a separate entity. As receiver for the *Grand Trunk Pacific, I intend in due course to present a detailed report of the operation [DOT]of that line for 1919, though I shall refer briefly to the results of that operation at a later stage of my present remarks.
The operating revenue of the National system as already stated, was more than ninety-three million dollars. The wage bill for the year exceeded seventy-three millions, having, owing largely to the McAdoo series of advances, jumped from fifty-four millions in 1918. In other words, out of every one dollar of revenue earned, seventy-eight cents passed directly, by way of *wages, to the employees.
Labour Conditions.
The cessation of hostilities . appreciably relieved the labour situation and enabled a start to be made on overtaking considerable maintenance of way and equipment work which had been deferred under war conditions. An extra large number of tie renewals were made, which, at the higher price and higher cost of labour, made a large item. Also relaying of rails which could not be gone on with during the war, added to operating expenses. Special locomotive, car, and work equipment repairs were undertaken with a view to keeping in service as much equipment as possible so as to avoid purchase of new units at the extraordinarily high prices to which I shall refer later.
It is to be remembered then, in dealing with the operating expenses for the year under review, that such deferred maintenance work as has been done, amounting to [DOT]over five million dollars, is included in the year's operating expenses, and to that extent has increased the deficit. There is still a large amount of deferred work to do, which will add to the operating costs for the year nineteen-twenty, but it is satisfactory to know that all the work which is being done is increasing the physical value of the property, as well as making for higher efficiency and economic operation.
The position of the 55,000 employees of the National system was materially improved during the year. They worked on the average a shorter day, and capital expenditures for the year included large items for the improvement of their housing and working conditions. In 1914 the average wage per year of the railway employees of Canada was $700; in 1919 on the National system it was $1,447.
The relations between the management and the employees have been very satisfactory. Since Canadian Railway Board of Adjustment No. 1 was established in September, 1918, Canadian railways have been remarkably free from serious labour troubles, and although the National system then comprised 35 per cent of the mileage in Canada, the grievances arising therefrom amounted to only about 16 per cent of the cases before the board. It is hoped that this board, which is comprised of six representatives of the large railway labour brotherhoods and six railway officers, will be maintained so that differences of opinion may continue to be settled by round table conference rather than by more expensive uneconomic and inconvenient methods.
Betterments.
Important progress was made during the year in improving the transportation plant of the Government-owned lines. The aim-of the management is to bring the lilies up to the standard which existing traffic justifies, and to improve these standards as traffic increases, and finally to reach the position where the facilities will provide a slight margin over the immediate traffic requirements, so that when emergency traffic develops there will not be congestion. With respect to many sections of the main lines this margin of capacity now exists, but expenditures are required on various sections, and at terminal and other important points where limiting conditions now restrict the economic handling of traffic. To improve track conditions, 625 miles of new 85 pound rail were laid, and on 130 additional miles of track the existing rail was replaced with heavier section, this-being largely good 80 or 70 pound rail released by the first item. The balance of the released rail was used up on the construction of 64 new passing tracks, and the extension of 35 others; also 44 transfer,

storage and other tracks, and 46 private and industrial tracks. This additional trackage will greatly facilitate the handling of trains and switching in yards.
About $1,200,000 was spent on ballasting. Over 100 trestles were replaced with permanent structures, and many other bridge improvements were made, a large item being $267,000 expended on the St. Charles river bridge. Good progress was made on the important work of providing a second track where in previous years serious congestion has occurred on the Intercolonial railway. The points where double tracking is being undertaken are between Ste. Rosalie and Charlotte, Truro and Belmont, between Springhill Junction and Maccan and also out of Moncton. Over a million dollars was expended on the work during 1919. The double track between Drumheller and Munson Junction, Alberta, has been completed, thus greatly facilitating the handling of coal from the Drumheller mines. In the case of the Drumheller work the grouping of 23 mines in one locality and the attendant mining conditions make the handling of the traffic practically a limiting factor in jiroduction; the movement, too, being crowded into a relatively short season, makes it imperative that good facilities for handling be provided. These expenditures to improve operating conditions produce in many cases a much greater return on the investment than equal expenditures on new lines, as not only are additional earnings secured, but operating expenses are reduced, greater use of equipment is obtained and better service to the fillblic. In line with the mahagement's policy of improving existing facilities, many new structures have been erected, among these being 16 wa'ter tanks, 11 coal handling plants, 2 coaling trestles, 26 stations, 12 station shelters, 13 freight sheds, 4 express buildings, 64 single section houses, 10 double section houses, 36 bunk houses, and 8 workmen's cottages. Such expenditures eliminate train delays, effect labour saving, add needed facilities, provide housing and tend to the welfare of employees.
Additions and improvements to round houses, machine shops and other mechanical facilities accounted for $125,000. General improvements included considerable ditching, widening banks, removing sags preparatory in some cases to ballasting. Some diversions to reduce grades, to give better alignment, or eliminate bridges were completed and others are under way.
[Mr. J. D. Reid.l
The rebuilding of the Canadian Northern line between Cap Rouge and Portneuf, washed out by the tidal wave in 1918, was almost completed.
On Prince Edward Island, where the lines are narrow gauge, a third rail has been laid from Charlottetown to Summer-side, and from Port Borden to Emerald- 60 miles in all, which enables standard gauge rolling stock to be interchanged by car ferry, greatly facilitiating the handling of traffic to and from the Island.
New Construction in 1919.
In submitting the construction programme for 1919, the directors recommended that the work to be undertaken should be as closely as possible confined to completing branch lines which were under construction in Western Canada at the outbreak of the war. Following this policy, work was done on various lines, among the more important being the extension of the Hanna-Medicine Hat line to Red Cliff, and the St. Paul de Metis line in Alberta, and the Humboldt-Melfort connection and Duck Lake branch in Saskatchewan, and in British Columbia the Kamloops-Kelowna line. On Vancouver island, twenty-eight miles of track were laid on grade previously constructed, and forty miles of ballasting completed. The Vancouver passenger station was completed and opened for traffic.
Shortage of labour and disturbed industrial conditions during the summer prevented the expected completion of certain Western branches, but the work on these will be vigourously- pushed this season.
At Toronto, the Leaside terminal yard was further developed. Most of the facilities at this point are now utilized and are proving of great value in handling the business on the lines in Southern Ontario.
Betterments Proposed for 1920.
The following general improvements are recommended by the directors as being among the most pressing requirements oi the system:	.
Canadian Government Railways.
The relaying of about 200 miles of track with heavier steel, and the utilization oi the released steel for additional passing tracks, spurs and sidings.
The completion of the 20 miles of double tracking already referred to and now well under way. Improvements to or replacing of over 200 bridges, trestles and culverts, including filling and other permanent work.
The construction of &5 stations and freight sheds, 7 coaling plants, 7 water

stations, nine buildings for the mechanical department such as engine houses, machine shops, etc., 58 buildings for housing employees such as section houses.
Provision will be made for the general improvement of track conditions, and at St. John an extension of the yard trackage is required, to relieve the congestion at that point.
Canadian Northern Lines.
The construction of branch line mileage in Western Canada provides an opportunity to replace steel now on main lines with heavier section, the steel taken from the main lines being serviceable for branch line traffic. The additional traffic being provided by the branch lines is enabling heavier train movements to be made, and the present demand for all-steel passenger equipment requires the utilization of very heavy power, making it necessary to continually improve the standard of main line roadbed, track and structures.
The programme in respect to rail replacements covers the relaying of 350 miles of new steel on main lines; 331 bridges, trestles aftd culverts are to be replaced, filled or renewed, involving the replacing of many temporary structures by permanent work. The completion of additional mileage in the Prairie Provinces has necessitated the construction of many new buildings, a large item being 68 new stations and freight sheds. There were also built 22 coaling plants. The present price of labour necessitates the adoption of labour-saving devices of this kind. There are also listed 20 new water stations. The mechanical department's facilities will be improved by the construction of new engine houses, machine shops, etc., 19 in all. Some of these are required at the end of new branch lines. Additional lines also account for a number of the 134 section houses required.
A large appropriation is required for general road-bed and track improvements and increasing traffic. warrants improvements and revision of the main line between 'Montreal and Quebec.	.
A greatly needed improvement is the stringing of an additional copper and steel wire between Montreal and Toronto and Winnipeg to provide through wires between these important points, the present wires being required for local business and train despatching. The new wires will also enable new through business to be handled by the G. N. W. through Canada, whereas the company's through business now goes via United States connections.
Construction Programme, 1920.
It is again proposed to confine new construction in Western Canada to the completion of branch lines on which work is well under way. The programme includes work on 16 branch lines in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. The principal items of track-laying will be from Eston south-easterly 35 miles; Humboldt-Melfort line, 32 miles; Melfort north-easterly, 32 miles; Oliver northeasterly, 22 miles; Peace River line, 324 miles; Swift Current line, 18J miles, and Jackfish Lake branch, 27 miles. In British Columbia it is proposed to grade 40.4 miles to complete the Okanagan branch. In all, 349.6 miles of track is to be laid and 123.4 miles of line to be graded. The extension of other lines and the construction of additional branches is very strongly urged, and while certain of these projections are fully justified on traffic considerations, their construction has to be postponed on account of the financial situation, labour shortage and high cost of material and supplies.
In Eastern Canada there are several very important connections which can be regarded as essential to economic and unified operation with other lines of the National system,- but which must also be postponed until the financial situation improves. Among these -may be mentioned the Long Lake connection between the National Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern main lines which, when completed, will give the Canadian Northern railway the short route between Winnipeg, Montreal and Toronto.

Passenger earnings have shown such a good increase that 30 additional heavy passenger locomotives are required, and 60 additional passenger train cars.
On account of the very high unit prices of rolling stock, the requirements have been kept down to the lowest point consistent with'traffic conditions. speechtext:
I will be glad to give any information that is desired as soon as we are in Committee of Supply.
The Question of Rates.
The question of rates is one which will bear careful examination. No system can indefinitely stand the relationship at, present existing between earnings and oper-
[Mr. J. D. Reid.l
ating expenses of the National, but before proceeding to a consideration of future rates, it may be wrell to review what has taken place in recent years in that connection. Hon. members will recall the agitation, extending over a period of years, for a reduction of rates in Western Canada, by many urged because it wras felt one railw'ay at least could well afford a reduction. Just a few months before the outbreak of w'ar this western rate case was finally decided. The judgment involved a comprehensive reduction in rates in territory w'est of the Great Lakes, and very seriously affected the new'er lines. Then came the w'ar and w'ith it undreamed of problems of transportation, and the railways began to feel the effects of war conditions. In 1916 what is known as the Eastern rates case provided for a five per cent increase in tariffs of Eastern roads, both Canadian and American, but it did not apply to the West. In 1918 there w'ere tw'o rate increases, the March order, commonly called the 15 per cent- increase, and the August increase of 25 per cent (so-called) which accompanied the first of the McAdoo series of wage increases. There was this difference, how'ever, between the rate increases and the wage increases: the latter were retroactive the rates could not be retroactive; and, in-addition, it wras found that the rate increases, w'hen finally applied, did not produce anything like the increase in revenue hoped for. The first mentioned (15 per cent) netted only seven per cent on the National Railw'ay system's passenger revenue and ten per cent on the system's freight r'evenue, or nine per cent on the gross. The second increase was on freight only, and w'as less in the West than in the East, ow'ing to the equalization of eastern and western rates involved. For instance, in Western Canada the 25 per cent increase wiped out the previous 15 per cent increment. Taken together, these two rate increases are estimated therefore to have approximately only 30 per cent instead of considerably more than 40 as they wrnuld have had they been imposed upon the other.
Now', there are only two ways by which a railway's revenues may be increased. One is by increased rates and the other is by increased business. The Canadian National railways, should-in view of the resumption of trade and immigration, in view' of the strengthening of w'eak spots by the inclusion of Grand Trunk lines, and especially in view of the traffic possibilities of the sixty steamships, the freight of w'hich will come to National railways,-commence to show a steady increase in business, but the

'management has, in the course of public utterances, called attention to the necessity for increased rates if operating expenses are to be met out of earnings. There are and will be various opinions as to this, but it behooves us to give careful consideration to the viewpoint of the management. They point out that Canadian roads are closely bound up with American roads, in proof of which witness the application of the McAdoo awards to Canada. Not only do we pay the same wage schedules and apply the same working conditions, but, generally speaking, freight rates are the same on both sides of the line. In the United States the roads are being handed back to their owners in groups, and the legislation provides that they be allowed to earn 5| per cent on their investments, with an additional half per cent construction betterments. During the war the American roads were guaranteed a certain return which was made up from the Public Treasury. Now that this guarantee no longer applies, either an increase in rates will be necessary or the American Government must continue to implement the earnings of the weaker roads. It is estimated that a rate increase of 26 per cent would be required to put the American roads on a paying basis. An increase to that extent, if applied to the earning of 1919 on the National system, would have produced a revenue of a little more than one hundred and ten millions, which would have left a surplus of net earnings of over two millions. That, of course, does not take the fixed charges into account. The management, therefore, feel that, both because we have the same expenditures to meet and must compete with each other all along the line, whatever freight increase is permitted in the United States ought also to be applied to Canadian roads. As Minister of Railways and having asked the management to operate on a business basis, I am bound to present the management's viewpoint for the consideration of Parliament.
I have, however, a larger responsibility as Minister of Railways, having, as such, to do with all Canadian roads, and answerable, in the final analysis, to the people, who at present find the cost of commodities sufficiently high. The railway situation in Canada has undergone a marked change, the entire mileage being now controlled in two great groups or systems, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. In Canada the mileage of the latter road is 14,824, but there are 4,948 of owned or controlled lines in the United States, so that 55
the system mileage aggregates 19,772. Including the Grand Trunk lines, the Canadian National system will comprise 22,356 miles, of which 2,093 miles are located in the States. These two great systems are, from the mileage standpoint, at any rate, fairly evenly balanced^ and it is unnecessary to point out to honourable members that ahy increase in rates granted ithe Canadian National system would equally apply to Canadian Pacific lines. No doubt, honourable members read in the newspapers recently the annual statement of this immense corporation, which showed that, notwithstanding the disadvantage of increased operating costs and charges common to all roads, the Canadian Pacific railway had been able to pay a dividend of seven per cent on their railway operation and three per cent on their outside operations, or in all their usual 10 per cent dividend on last year's operation.
Now, the argument has been advanced that it would be possible to tax out of the Canadian Pacific Railway any increase in earnings which might be permitted them in common with the Canadian National system. T have my own opinion as to the fairness of such a proposition, but, in any event, I personally feel that such a proposal, even if fair from the standpoint of competition, would not be practicable, for the simple reason that you could not prevent the Canadian Pacific from spending their revenue legitimately on the improvement. of their property, and if, at the end of the year, we found that the increased earnings had gone into betterments, how could we tax it out of them?
My own feeling is that the Canadian Pacific are entitled to a rate sufficient to earn 7 per cent on their Tailway investment, and this they appear to be able to do, notwithstanding present abnormal conditions. The question resolves itself, therefore, into the following proposition:
Shall Canadian freight rates be increased generally for the particular purpose of enabling the Canadian National system to meet its operating expenses and fixed charges, or would it be better to go on with the present rates, giving dealers no additional excuse for increasing the cost of living, and trusting to increase in business, the economies it should be possible to effect by co-ordination, and the return of normal conditions to gradually reduce these deficits until the day (which I personally feel is not far off) when the revenue will prove sufficient to pay for operation and, later, also to take care of fixed charges?



Should this latter suggestion prevail, it would require to be thoroughly understood that the Minister ol Railways, no matter who he may be, must oome down next year with a deficit, and the next year with a deficit, and so on for a few years until we shall have turned the comer.
The earnings of the Canadian Railways last year were 350 millions, made up as follows:

A 25 per cent increase on these earnings would approximate $88,000,000, the greater part of which would be earned in Canada. Whether we shall take 88 millions in increased freight fates out of the people of the country next year in order to show a surplus for the National system is a question as to which I myself am not prepared to take the responsibility of deciding either one way or the other at the present time. I leave it to the consideration of the House and of the people of Canada as a whole, and shall be glad to elicit representative public opinion in the matter, so that the Government may be in a position to give this important question the best possible consideration.
Bringing in the Grand Trunk.
The current year will witness the rounding out of the Canadian National Railway system by the acquisition of the Grand Trunk and its subsidiary lines. With these added, it is estimated that over 50 per cent of the domestic freight traffic of the Dominion will be found to originate along Government railways. The connecting up of the Grand Trunk lines will give direct access to eastern industrial centres, especially in Ontario. Western Canadian business originating on Grand Trunk lines will no longer require to be split into three but can go forward in one long haul over all-National lines, and, vice versa, the Grand Trunk will benefit from a large amount of additional business from our Western lines which it could not obtain except as a member of the National system.
Pear has been expressed that Halifax and St. John might suffer as a result of the * Government taking over the Grand Trunk. The people of Eastern Canada need have no fear of this for the reason that these are the terminals of our immense railway systems and have been for many years. They have been greatly improved, and in 
the operation of our National system, more especially in view of the ocean tonnage we now control, these ports will become increasing, rather than diminishing, factors in the Canadian railroad situation.
The connecting up of the Grand Trunk lines will mean that 52 per cent of the entire railway mileage of Canada will have passed under Government control. This will permit of economies in operation where the two systems have been maintaining parallel lines and duplicate staffs, and, as already pointed out, there should be compensating advantages to the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial and the Grand Trunk as well. I wish to point out, however, that, in speaking of advantages, I am referring to the Grand Trunk lines only, not the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Transcontinental Railway systems. These last named colonization roads, built as part and parcel of the Grand Trunk, are bound to be unprofitable for many years to come. The loss on operation of the Transcontinental last year was $2,735,000. This was included in the Canadian National figures already referred to. But there is also the Grand Trunk Pacific, which the Government found on its doorstep in 'March oi last year, and as to the operation of which I shall have to make a separate report, as the figures form no part of the National system figures with which we have been dealing. But to make my present statement complete, I desire to point out that the Grand Trunk Pacific for the year ending December 31 last showed an operating loss of five and a half millions. To this must be added fixed charges of eight and a half millions, making a total deficit of fourteen millions, an increase of three and a half millions over 1918. The reasons for this increase was set out in a communication from the General Manager to myself as Receiver, and these will be dealt with at the proper time.
Personally, I do not think it will be possible for many years to make the expenses of operating these colonization roads, nor do I think it fair that they should be expected to make the showing we look for from the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial or the Grand Trunk proper. Therefore, I think the annual loss on these railways should not be added to the net deficit of the Canadian National railways for purposes of comparison, and I have instructed the management that the operation of these systems must be shown separately at the close of each year, so that when comparisons are made between other systems and

our Government system, the comparison may be a reasonably fair one.
Hudson Bay Railway.
There is one more railway which was commenced and which has not been completed, which is known as the Hudson Bay railway. For the information of the hon. members, I may say that the Government has decided that no more work shall be done on that during the coming year. It is the intention to use every effort to extend branch lines into districts where settlers are much more in evidence and in much gieater need of railway communication. The Hudson Bay Railway will therefore stand until financial conditions will permit of its resumption.
In conclusion let me say there was a time, not long ago, when the Government system was largely a local carrier getting the short end of business that goes with the short haul. The longest haul it could Hope for was from Halifax or Sydney to Montreal, and vice versa. And in competing with the Grand Trunk for Montreal business offering to the seaboard, we could charge only the Portland rate, though the Intercolonial mileage to Halifax was 841 as against the Grand Trunk's 297 to Portland. Similarly, the Canadian Pacific railway had the advantage of its comparatively short haul of 481 miles to St. John, and for business originating at the Intercolonial chief terminal, Halifax, it had to compete with this same highly organized and stronger competitor, whose agents were always active abroad and whose ships were ever on the seas. But a change has come over the scene. Now the Government system itself bestrides the continent, with branches reaching for the first time into productive centres and with terminals upon both Eastern and Western oceans. The story of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine has been told by the proper minister, and at last we also have our ships upon the seas, and our agents abroad will actively compete for international trade. Keen competition, " adroit, persistent, aggressive and fair," is promised by the President of the Canadian Pacific, who expresses the hope that both their own systems and the National may in future work in common for the advancement of the country. He says there need no longer be controversy, but that there will always be keen competition. That is what the management of the National system expects and welcomes. I am told that the nationalization of the Canadian Northern has made no difference in the morale of the employees of that road, that they are as keenly alert as ever and " on their toes to make government ownership and operation a success. We expect the employees of the Grand Trunk systems will co-operate with equal loyalty, and the (Government in turn will spare no effort to build up a great National railway system able to compete with and maintain the high standard of transportation efficiency reached by the Canadian Pacific. That road may well be the standard against which we may measure the success of government ownership and operation. I say " success " because I am not prepared for one moment to contemplate any other possibility. The National lines, with the Grand Trunk included, will comprise a system which will (Serve every province in Canada, which is identified with every progressive community, and- must continue to perform the major part of the transportation service of the entire Dominion. We have taken steps to remove the Government's lines from political interference. Experienced railway men are in charge; they are being .given money to improve the roadbed, to ,buy the best equipment to enable the greatest tonnage' to be hauled in a single train. It is the greatest encouragement towards expansion to have this great National system ready and equipped to handle additional traffic as it develops-and it surely will develop. If we imagine Canada to have reached the maximum of development then we shall have planned foolishly, but I, for one, have the faith to feel and the vision to prophesy that this great transportation system is not being prepared to perform this splendid transportation service in vain.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. minister's address will, I think, confirm the opinion generally held throughout the country that the Government have absolutely no railway policy. He has just stated to us, if I caught his figures correctly, that we made a loss on operation of $14,000,000 and a loss on interest charges of $19,000,000, or a total loss of $33,000,000, and that no provision whatever for maintenance is included in these figures. So that he comes down to us to-day with a statement showing that if we had maintained the road properly we would have sustained a loss this year of not less than $60,000,000; and he tells us also that this loss is to be continued for one year, perhaps for two or more years, perhaps for many years to come. He states in his usual way that he has no policy as to what is to be done about this deficit: Whether he is going to ask the people to continue to pay these heavy losses [DOT] out of the treasury of the country or whether he is going to adjust his management so that the road will earn the revenues that it should earn. The minister did not say a word, so far as I heard, about the management. Apparently he is. quite satisfied to let the Mackenzie and Mann crowd go on tapping the treasury of Canada indefinitely. He is not prepared to tax the people who are using the service; he is quite willing that the Mackenzie and Mann crowd should go on spending this $50,000,000 or $60,000,000 a year without giving any information whatever to this House or to the country. The amount that the minister mentions is only the deficit; no account is taken of expenditures necessary for maintenance or for betterments. During the past two or three years we have spent huge sums on this system, and all that we can get from the minister to-day is that we may expect to go on spending forty, fifty, sixty or more millions per annum until these railroad barons, these Canadian robbers, shall have exhausted the treasury of this country.
The minister stated that colonization roads were not paying. I am glad to see the leader of the Government (Sir George Foster) in his seat, because I wish to direct his attention to a matter with regard to *colonization roads that is of prime importance to every Canadian. We have developed in the northern part of Quebec a railway system and we have settled in that country upwards of 15,000 of the best colonizers that can be found anywhere in the world; they are the only people who will ever colonize the northern part of our Canadian domain. They are not like the people who were being
(Mr. Deputy Speaker.]
taken out of Kapuskasing during the last few months; they are doing successful work in the district in which they have settled. The only drawback is the lack of railway facilities. I wish to read an affidavit which I received from there a few days ago. It is signed by Frank Blais, and reads as follows :
I,	the undersigned, Erank Blais, lumber merchant. of the village of Amos, make oath and say:
1.	There is actually at the different sidings between La Heine and Nottaway-
That is a very short distance in that country.	.
-on the Transcontinental railway, more than 60,000 cords of pulp wood piled up ready to be shipped.
2.	There is also in this same district 20,000,000 feet of sawn lumber ready to be forwarded which was left in the yards from 1919 on account of the shortage of cars, and there will be about 60,000,000 more manufactured during next season.
3.	It would need about 6,500 cars to ship the lumber and pulp wood already piled up ready to be forwarded.
4.	The authorities of the Transcontinental have only placed at the disposition of the owners of the pulp wood and lumber about 50 cars during the whole month of February, and about the same proportion during this month of March.
5.	When the cars are loaded and moved from our sidings, they only reach their destination point after a delay of six or eight weeks, and often more.
6.	The employees of the railroad will not take the trouble of placing the cars on the sidings in the proper way to be used conveniently by the shippers, and the engines used do not seem to be in the proper state to give satisfaction in moving the cars.
7.	The whole Abitibl region is suffering heavy losses from the facts above mentioned.
And I have signed:
Frank Blais.
Sworn before me at Amos this 22nd day of March, 1920.
C. A. Lafrance, N.P.,
Com. Supreme Court. District of Quebec.
Now, there is the condition of the road that the minister states lost traffic last year on account of the war being over. He says that the earnings were decreased because the railways did not have the traffic; yet here is traffic lying right at hand that has not been moved. I want to read the letter accompanying the affidavit, because it throws light on this subject, and there is a good deal of truth in it. It reads:
Again we have to apply for your protection and to ask you to take our interests in hand. I am writing in my own name, but I will send you declarations by other lumber merchants and pulp wood dealers, which shall prove to you that the same unfortunate situation exists all over the Abitibi region. We believe this

state of affairs could be improved with your help, by putting the case before the authorities of the Federal Government, which has full control over this situation.
You are perfectly aware of the fact that the pulpwood and lumber trades are the only sources of revenue for this part of the county. To take advantage of this industry we necessarily need cars for the transportation of the lumber and pulpwood, and we actually have no cars of no kind for that purpose. We are asking such cars through all the officers of the railway, with no result.
I have myself over 15,000 cords of pulpwood, at a cost of more than $120,000, and I can get no cars to forward the same. I have made a demand for 30 cars a day, and I received an average of one car per day. In two months from now all that wood we own will be exposed to burn in the bush fires, and we could not sustain such a loss. The money has been advanced by the banks, who are helping us to buy that pulpwood from the settlers, who have no other means to support their families. It would also be a total loss for the paper mills, that are already blamed on account of the high price charged for their paper. We have been compelled to stop buying any pulpwood, not being able to ship what we have on hand, and there is still a great quantity for sale by settlers, who are waiting on such sale to support their families.
There is in the Abitibi region about 55,000 cords of pulp wood to be shipped before the bush fires become a danger and it would need about 4,000 cars.
There was about 20,000,000 feet of lumber left from 1919 on account of the shortage of cars and there will be about 60,000,000 feet more during next season, which will need about 5,500 cars for expedition and we are wishing that you would ask the Federal authorities to prepare for such expedition of lumber and to provide for the actual need of cars for pulp wood.
. You will probably have as an answer that there is no cars to be had, but I can assure you the contrary and as an example let me tell you that in February last, at Hearst, west of Cochrane, there were enough cars loaded there to force an embargo on the shipments of pulpwood from that place and there were more cars loaded than could be received; while in that same month of February my requisition was for 30 cars a day and all I had during the whole month was 6 cars.
I believe the officers of the railway in our region are doing their best to help us, but their instructions come from a higher source that does not seem to sympathize with our requirements.
Every year there are thousands of cords of pulpwood burned by the settlers who cannot sell such wood on account of the shortage of cars. This is a serious loss and we believe that the situation could be very much improved if the Federal authorities are willing to do so.
Mr. Speaker, the intimation in this letter is that the Federal Government are deliberately trying to kill settlement in the Abitibi district. It is well known that the members of the present Government who were in Opposition when the road was built opposed its construction, and it is well known that they have since taken every
means of opposing the development of that country. I want to ask the leader of the Government-I am tired asking the Minister of Railways and the Department of Railways for help in that district-if it is the studied policy of the Government to choke that district off; if it is their determination to see that the settlers have no means of subsistence? Or will the Government see that these people get relief? The railways of the country cannot possibly succeed if this kind of management prevails throughout Canada. We are told by the minister that they do not succeed. Well, scarcely any person expected anything else. Having regard to the present system of no management for the railway and no railway policy on the part of the Government, how can we hope that the Canadian National railways will succeed?
I shall not take up any further time until I have had an opportunity of studying the minister's statement. But I do hope that before this discussion proceeds the minister will lay down some definite policy for the management of these railways.

If the minister will answer definitely a question which I have put to him by correspondence and on the floor of this House, I will refrain from laying my grievances before the House on this occasion; otherwise I propose to make my speech. When will the Oliver-St, Paul de Metis railway be completed so that a service may be afforded to people who have been suffering from lack of railway facilities since 1909?

I thought perhaps if I mentioned what I was going to take up the minister would be able to say whether he was going to deal with that question or not; and if not, I was going to make a complaint on account of a promise made by the minister last year. I do not know whether I am in order or not. I wanted to make a statement as to what I wished to complain about. If the minister is going to deal with that question, I am quite willing to wait until the House goes into Commttee of Supply.

Last year before the Railway Committee the minister promised, at a time when the Canadian Pacific were applying for a charter for a line parallelling the line of the Canadian National railway, that if they would withdraw, and the committee, instead of supporting the charter of the Canadian Pacific for a Jine to parallel the line of the Canadian National railway, would give the department an opportunity, they would guarantee to build a road from Whitford to Bruderheim. The Canadian Pacific had arranged to extend their line from Cutknife to Whitford and wished to extend it to South Edmonton. I may say, in passing, that Whitford is an old thickly populated settlement, a settlement that has been in existence for some thirty-five years. Every odd or even section is under cultivation in the whole district, and a delegation came here, sent by the people from that * district, they naturally being very anxious to have railway facilities. There were present that day in the railway committee Mr. D. C. Coleman, Vice-President of the Canadian Pacific, and Mr. McLeod of the Canadian Northern, and it was . arranged amongst them that day that the Canadian
[Mr. Deputy Speaker.!
Pacific would be allowed to extend their line through Lloydminster to Whitford and the Canadian Northern would extend on their old charter from Whitford to Bruderheim, thereby relieving the people in that section of the country. The minister at that time promised that the railroad would be built last year. I might say that at that time Mr. MoLeod stated that the line of the railroad had been graded some four miles. II took the opportunity then to point out that the grading had been started, but that very part of the road that he claimed was under construction was now being farmed and under crop. The minister, however, promised that that extension would be constructed to relieve those people, but not a sod has been turned and nothing has been done along that line. That is why I rose to ask if any provision was made in the minister's programme that the construction of that road should go on this summer. That is what I wanted to bring before the House and the minister.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I quite understand that we have some latitude when we come into committee and deal with specific items. Nevertheless, the minister himself found it necessary to make his statement while you, Sir, occupied the Chair, and when we have a wider range of discussion, as he might possibly find any particular item too narrow for the statement which he found it necessary to make. In like manner, I presume that private members of the House will find it necessary, in order' to deal in a general way, with the statement made by the minister and the matters of policy which that statement contains, to deal with this question perhaps a little more at length while the Speaker is in the Chair and the matter is before the House as such.
For the last number of years we have heard a great deal about railway policies, railway ownership, private ownership and public ownership. I have been following the different changes that have been taking place in this House and in the country with regard to railways for some twenty years past; and the Government of the day and the party behind it take much glory to themselves because they say that they are big Canadians in connection with railway policies, and that they have a big policy in connection with railway matters. Speaking for myself, I have always contended and I still contend that the proper way to do railway business or any other business that can be

left to a private concern, is to have it done in that way. I have always contended that, whatever the reason may be, it is impossible to get oiut of men and measures and policies in the hands of Governments the same satisfactory results as we get from private ownership and enterprise. This country of ours is the same from coast to coast, it is the same from the American boundary to the north for everbody that is in it; at least, we hope that that is the case; that there is no discrimination; that there is no favouritism. We hope that there are no shackles thrown around the neck or limbs of any person who is in business. We find in this same Canada a corporation, to which reference has been made to-day, doing splendid business, extending their lines, keeping their lines in first-class shape with everything going along well, and in the adverse conditions with which they have had to deal within the last year, they come down with a dividend of 10 per cent upon the operations of the year. That is private business, that is the management of some 22,000 miles of railway in the hands of private men, men who have grown up in the business, men who are trained, men who have nothing else in view but the business of the company, and the company is making money. That is one side of the matter; that is the side which I have always advocated, the side that I stand by. It was flung at us last year by hon. gentlemen opposite that we were the enemies of the country because we did not jump at this idea of Government-owned railways and Government management of railways in this country. If any evidence were required to show that Government management of and Government enterprise in railways in this country are a huge failure, we had that evidence in the most conclusive manner from the statement in its very best form that was given to the House to-day. The statement made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) to-day bears at every line, at every turn and at every page, the earmarks of the special pleader, the preparation, not of the minister, but of those who are under him, those who are trying to make the most of a bad bargain, and to make appear in the very best light the jumble of figures, the jumble of lines, the jumble of management which is foisted upon this country and which burden we have to shoulder. If I wanted to present the worst example of Government management of a railway or any other enterprise, I have it here. We are told that there is a deficit of something like $95,000,000 or $100,000,000, but
that figure merely touches the fringe of the truth, as we should find if we had it. There is nothing said about what must be expended on these lines to put them in such shape that we can compete with our great competitor in this country. What can one say? What can one suggest? I would say to the Canadian people, if it were possible; get from under this burden as quickly as you can. Get it in business-like shape as soon as you can. Get it under proper management and try and make it work its way along; let one hand wash the other, so to speak. That is what any sane person with any sense of responsibility would say, if there were any means of bringing it about. I presume, however, that having been exploited for the last twenty or twenty-five years by private owners, who have kept running to their friends in this House and in this Government and have been getting all the money they required to make millions for themselves, the roads are in such a condition to-day that no private enterprise would take this monstrosity off our hands on anything like fair terms. We, therefore, have to make the most of the -situation, and try and get the enterprise into business-like shape, putting all our energy behind it. It is now some, two years since we were rushed here to pass an Act of Parliament for the purpose of creating some, corporation that was to take hold of these roads. Politics were to be thrown to the winds, we were told. There was such a rush to get that legislation through Parliament that before the Bill was printed closure was applied in this House. You will hardly believe it, Mr. Speaker, but five pages of printed matter were added to the Bill after the closure had been on for twenty or thirty-six hours. The enterprise was so big, and the responsibility so great and pressing, that the Government could not wait one minute to put these roads into the hands of this corporation that was to be created. Well, the legislation passed. Summer came, then winter, then another summer and winter, and now I think we are getting near the close of the third year since that Bill was passed, and yet no action has been taken by the Government under that legislation. Nobody has been appointed, and things are pulling along just as they please. We are supposed to have a business 'Government, a business Minister of Railways, a business-like management all around. We are told we have these things, but what do we find when we look in the next? It is very nice, if a man is running a hennery, to have fine hens, but

you want to look in the nest to find if there are any eggs, to see what results these birds of beautiful plumage which you are feeding, and feeding highly are giving. When we look at the nest in connection with this railway we find it is like Mother Hubbard's Cupboard-always empty. We are feeding it highly, but the balance is always on the wrong side. We get no results. How long is this to continue? I appeal to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways whether he is satisfied with this condition of things. I do not think he is. I think he says to this management from year to year, before presenting his statement to Parliament: Prepare this monstrous nightmare yourself. It is bad enough for me to be obliged to read it, but I will go into the House, supported perhaps by a glass of whiskey or something, and I will read it.
Take it back.
This is a dry country.

Perhaps it is. It was certainly a dry statement. There is nothing personal, however, to be said in connection with this undertaking. It is too crushing a load to be put on the back of any one person. I appeal to the people of this country and to the management of this system, if there is anybody responsible among them, to see if something cannot be done to take the enterprise along lines where there will be a show of daylight at some stage. The Minister of Railways tells us we are going to get around the corner. That is a wonderful soit of corner. It reminds me of the fool jackass that had a tuft of hay put on the end of a pole tied around its neck with a rope, so that the tuft of hay was always ten feet ahead of him. We seem to be getting further away from this corner all the time instead of approaching it, and we are spending millions upon millions of the people's money in the process, without any hope of ever getting it back. That is the position to-day. Without going into details just now, let me hope that there may be a prospect of reaching this corner, which seems to be so extremely difficult to get at. It took Moses forty years to get to the Promised Land, and it looks as if it was going to take us an equal number of years to put our hands on this corner which the minister is holding out to us, where better things will be in prospect for the people of this country.
We were told that the railways were to be taken clean out of politics, that politics was

to have nothing whatever to do with them; but what was the statement made to-day? The minister says that the management have no policy, they cannot determine what should be done. We must do one of two things, he says. We must continue to plunge into the pockets of the Canadian people, or we must dig into their pockets in another way by increasing the freight rates. The management, he says, have not got a policy; they have not the punch or the backbone to decide for themsleves, and so they ask me to decide. But I will not decide. I do not know what is to be done, so I will bring the matter back to this old political court, and you can do as you please about it. Is that getting away from politics? Are we not getting the railways back into politics worse than ever before? We were told that it cost this country some millions of dollars every year while we were trying to get the roads away from politics, and that in future politics would have nothing whatever to do with the roads. I say, Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) told this House last year and the year before, it is impossible for any road or any property that is owned and managed by the people of this country to get away from political influences. Even if it were possible, I would not be a party to it. So long as the people of this country are putting their money into any enterprise or are being taxed for the maintenance of any undertaking in this country, they should have an opportunity through their representatives in this Parliament of having something to say about it. To suggest that we can spend hundreds of millions of dollars of the people's money every year without the people having anything to say about it, is a most absurd and unworkable proposition, and the sooner we get back to rock bottom, and understand that the people of this country have a right to know what is being done with their money, the better. If we appoint a management to look after a railway or any other enterprise, that management must be answerable to the people of this country. This Parliament should have something to say about their appointment, and the Government should be perfectly frank and open with us, so that we may at the earliest possible moment know precisely what may be expected to be done. We cannot go on in this way, Mr. Speaker. I am sure that on either side of the House the minister could find wisdom, experience and the faculty^ of direction that would materially help him if he would only seek for these qualities.

, Now, Mr. Speaker, I think that at this stage it is perhaps in order for me to point out to the minister that the people in the part of the country from which I come think themselves entitled to at least fair consideration in matters of transportation. The section of the country which I have the honour to represent in this House is the oldest part of this great Canada of ours. In my county is the spot wheTe Cabot is supposed to have landed some two hundred years ago, and it is a matter for surprise, and some indignation, on calm reflection, that the splendid people in that part of Canada are 110 miles from the nearest railroad. The people are adept fishermen and successful farmers, but they lack transportation facilities. In 1911 the sum of $100,000 or thereabouts was placed in the Estimates in order to provide a start in railroad building down there, but when this Government came into power they wiped that Estimate out. They declined to do anything in the matter, promising instead to consider the situation at a later date. In 1914, the minister being in the House, I introduced a resolution to the effect that the time had arrived when something should be done to furnish with proper facilities the good people in the Island of Cape Breton, in the county of Victoria. My good friend accepted the resolution in 1914; but, the war intervening, I deemed it proper, in the national interest and in view of the exigencies of the crisis which had suddenly burst upon us, not to press my resolution at that time or during the war. Last year, however, I moved another resolution in the House expressing the view that, in the opinion of the House, the time had come when my former resolution of 1914 should be implemented, and urging upon the Government the imperative necessity for action. That resolution was accepted by the minister and the Government, but I regret to say that nothing has been done, not even a survey having been undertaken. I find that my hon. friend is extending lines west, buying new lines, and doing sundry works in various parts of the country for the purpose of improving the railway facilities of Canada. I have no fault to find with this programme, but I do say that it is now away past the time when the Government should implement its promises and carry forward a policy that was intended by previous Governments to be fully prosecuted. It is not to the credit of this Government that part of the railway policy of the Laurier Government in 1911 was ignored to suit their purposes. Every Tory road that was in contemplation at that time was built; but because this little road of mine in the good old county of Victoria happened to be in the constituency of an Opposition man, nothing has been done there. I submit that the good peole of my county should not be - punished and deprived of railway facilities simply because, of their free will and in the exercise of the franchise, they sent to the House of Commons a representative who does not happen to be sitting on the same side of the House as the Government. That should not be the policy of any Government; least of all should it be the policy of the Union Government. The policy of the Government should take cognizance of the best interests of every part of the country regardless of the political procliviities of any community. At a later stage, Mr. Speaker, I may have something further to say on this point.
I had the pleasure of meeting the minister in my own town of North Sydney some two years ago, when the hon. gentleman had an opportunity to see the congested condition of the chief terminus of the Intercolonial railway in Eastern Nova Scotia. He saw that the wharves were not large enough and that there was not enough space. There were more steamships in than there was space to accommodate them; and ten cars were ready to be pushed on the wharf where there was room for only one. Through that point goes out the immense traffic that Canada has built up with Newfoundland, and the minister was impressed with the great necessity that existed at that time, and that still exists, for attention to that terminus. Nothing has been done, however. As I heard the minister reciting the various improvements and extensions of facilities which are contemplated, I was astonished to hear nothing about this terminus at North Sydney. Probably it is not a matter of very great concern to us as to what are the requirements of the Dominion of Newfoundland, although we should have at heart the interests of every part of the 'Empire to which we belong. But at the same time the trade that has been built up between all parts of Canada -Winnipeg, Montreal, Toronto, Halifax, etc.-with Newfoundland is immense, and if we desire to maintain that trade and traffic we must have proper facilities at the terminus at North Sydney, so that people will not have to wait two or three months before getting freight through because of a lack of accommodation. It is not a matter of personal interest to me whether or not the trade goes through that

point, but it is in the interest of the whole of Canada that we should hold on to the enormous traffic which has already been built up. It is not always gratifying, although it sometimes affords a bit of satisfaction, to find one's prophecies and predictions fulfilled as time goes on. But I have always, in the face of opposition and of threats from hon. gentlemen opposite, maintained, as is apparent now, that the best way in which to deal with questions of a large character, such as the management of railways in this country, was by private enterprise if private enterprise were willing to take hold of the!', business. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me read a statement that was made by Lord Macaulay as far back as 1830, and which applies to this question of State ownership as compared with private enterprise. [DOT] Lord Macaulay said:
Our rulers will best promote the improvement of the nation by strictly confining themselves to their own legitimate duties, by leaving capital to find its most lucrative course, commodities their fair prices, industry and intelligence their natural reward, idleness and folly their natural punishment, by maintaining peace, by defending property, by diminishing the price of law, and by observing strict economy in every department of the State. Let the Government do this; the people will assuredly do the rest.
Although there were at that time few Government-owned railways, or indeed railways of any kind, there must have been other enterprises whose conduct led Lord Macaulay to make this wise statement, which is more or -less prophetic in its application to present day conditions. I submit to the best judgment of the Government this advice which the great British statesman gave so far back as the year 1830, and hope that the Government will do one of two things: Either organize some concern that will take this business out of their hands; or, if they will not do this, see to it themselves that proper management is put in charge of affairs so that we may have an institution that will at least pay its way, although it could not pay any interest on the huge sums of money which the people of Canada have invested in the enterprise with which we are now dealing.
Mr. ROBERT H. BUTTS (South Cape Breton and Richmond): I wish merely to contribute one or two observations to this debate. Listening to the speech of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat I was struck with the remarks he made with respect to railroad matters chiefly, and particularly in regard to Mackenzie and Mann. I would like to remind my hon. friend that
[Mr. McKenzie.!
the eggs that hatched out Mackenzie and Mann were hatched out in a Liberal nest; that the eggs which hatched out the Transcontinental railway were hatched out in a Liberal nest; and that the two knighthoods that were bestowed on Mackenzie and Mann likewise emanated from a Liberal nest. My hon. friend's remarks might come with very good grace from almost any member on this side of the House, but it ill behooves any hon. gentleman opposite to make such comments and remarks as my hon. friend has indulged in. Let me say in this connection, there is an old proverb that it is a dirty bird that soils its own nest.
With respect to the question of the terminals at Sydney and the facilities for handling the Newfoundland trade my hon. friend is perhaps as well, if not better, acquainted with conditions there than any one in this House. He says that hardly a day goes by that he does not pass those terminals, hardly a day that he does not find there, to a greater or less extent, a congestion of trade. That is true, but that congestion of trade is owing to the fact that the Reids' have never performed their end of the undertaking. They have got a nar-row-guage railway from Port aux Basques to St. John's and it takes their express train, if she runs on time, 28 hours to cover that distance. Now, you can imagine, gentlemen, if you were operating a line of boats that were able to carry away all the freight that goes to North Sydney how you would feel upon reaching Port aux Basques to discover there is not at that place room for its accommodation. I have been to Port aux Basques and seen the existing wharves and sufficient ships cannot be docked there to carry away the freight that is brought in the fall of the year, when the maximum amount of congestion occurs. Consequently the Reid people are obliged to put on extra boats. Those extra boats come directly from North Sydney where all the freight for Newfoundland is handled, but they do not go to Port aux Basques; they go to Placentia and St. John's directly, because the Reid railroad is not capable of handling all the freight that offers. Therefore before any complaint can be made against the railway and terminal facilities on Cabot Strait we should require the Reid-Newfoundland company to provide facilities for handling it on the other side. What is the use of taking freight down to Port aux Basques, when in the first place you can only dock your ship if the pier is vacated by the Reid-Newfoundland boats, and then only one at a time. And even if

you could dock your ships fast enough there is not sufficient storage room nor wharfage to take all the freight- offering. Even if there was sufficient dock accommodation there is not a railway capable of carrying the freight from there to Placentia or St. John's. Such are the actual conditions at the present time, I have hinted at the desirability of improvements at different times to the Minister of Railways, and I hopd he will take those hints into consideration, and that the day is near when instead of relying upon the Reids', the Canadian Government will take over the control of the facilities themselves, handle their own freight, and as far as possible their own passenger boats, running directly from Sydney harbour to Placentia or St. John's, and act independently of the Reid-New-foundland company. Then gentlemen, we will have a solution of the problem which awaits settlement down there. Until some action of that kind is taken no remedy will be afforded. Imagine a railway running from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Port aux Basques, through a territory of 520 odd miles and taking 28 hours to cover that distance, having to traverse a narrow-guage road so exposed at certain points that freight cars were blown off the track in the month of November.
Oh, oh.

It is not a thing to be
laughed at, gentlemen, the incident which I have mentioned actually occurred.
