These are the conditions that the Government have to face, and if the terminals at Sydney harbour are not large enough the best thing to do would be to cease relying upon the Reid-Newfoundland company and let this Government handle the traffic running directly from Sydney harbour to Placentia or St. John's, Newfoundland.

I am very pleased to have had the privilege of listening to the address of the Minister of Railways. It is always a pleasure for me to hear him, because he reminds me that whenever an advocate has a bad case if he speaks sufficiently loud and sufficiently long he can make that case appear somewhat presentable. The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) has described that policy as a little nebulous and I am inclined to think that was an appropriate characterization. Under the terms of the previous legislation the Government has acquired most of the Canadian railways with the exception of the Canadian Pacific railway. In the statement which he has
presented to-day the minister told us that he puts the Grand Trunk Pacific and Grand Trunk to one side because they do not show any profit on their operations. He says that this year and next year, and perhaps for two or three years, he will have to come to Parliament and ask for a vote of some millions from Parliament to cover probable deficits resulting from the operation of these railways and provide for the improvements which they may need. The minister, however, does not give us any indication as to these amounts which it will be necessary to provide from the Dominion Treasury. There is another point which impressed me very forcibly this afternoon, and that was when I heard the Minister of Marine reply to the hon. member for Quebec West, with respect to the loading of certain ships at the port of Quebec, The minister said: "We have nothing to do with this matter, it is in the hands of the Canadian Government Mercantile Marine Company.'' Practically the same reply was made' by the Minister of Railways on the same subject. In view of this attitude on the part of members of the Government we have this situation:	That although we are the shareholders, and are supposed to be the owners and stockholders of the Canadian National Railway System, members of the Government come here and declare that they know practically nothing about the operation of ships belonging to the Canadian people be-. cause the management of these vessels has been turned oyer to a limited corporation which alone is going to deal with the matter. '
There is another point to which I desire to draw the attention of the House and it is this:	Some days ago we heard that the
president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. D. B. Hanna, for whom I have a great respect, had stated in the course of an address at a certain meeting-I think it was reported in the press-that the Government should -keep their hands off the Canadian National Railway and its administration. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) has said the same thing, and hon. members on the other side of the House said the same thing when the Canadian National Railway Company was being incorporated. Whenever any of us have occasion to discuss any matter with the directorate we are told that the administration of the railway is in their hands, and that inasmuch as the people have placed them in control they-the directorate-are clothed with all the necessary powers in regard to operation and improvements. I object to this principle, Mr. COMMONS
Speaker, as I objected last year when the Canadian Northern Kailway Bill was before the House. We then protested against that policy, because it was equivalent to taking away from the people the right of being consulted as to the manner in which public money should be expended.
Although I may be called somewhat too parochial, Mr. Speaker, I hope that I may be allowed to discuss, while the policy of the Canadian National Kailways is before the House, certain matters which particularly concern the constituency which I have the honour to represent in this House, the county of Charlevoix-Montmorency. Some years ago the Government passed legislation for the acquisition of the Quebec and Saguenay Railway from a certain point in the county of Montmorency to another point in the county of Charlevoix. Last year the completed portion of the railway was operated from the first of July until November. Murray Bay, or as it is called "La Malbaie," is one of the greatest summer resorts in Canada, and at once a large freight and passenger business was opened up, with profitable results to the railway. But for one reason or another, in the month of November all of a sudden I heard that the Government had decided to discontinue the daily train service and run only three trains a week. I inquired of the minister the reason for this change, and was told that it was in the best interests, of the country as the service was sufficient for the locality. All the local public bodies as well as the big industrial companies settled in that part of the country protested against the change, and I hold in my hand petitions, letters and other documents of protest which were at that time lodged through me with the Minister of Railways and the president of the Canadian National Railways. I also wrote to these gentlemen, and in reply was told that the action complained of simply had to be taken.
Mr. Speaker, it is not very often that I congratulate the Gvoernment, but they are entitled to my congratulations on the service they maintained until the month of November, for the trains were well operated and were profitable to the Government. But from the first of November up to the present day only a restricted service has been continued, with the result that all the good effects which followed from the daily train service are not in evidence to-day. I bring up this point in the hope that the Minister >of Railways (Mr. Reid) will evolve a new policy in regard to that train service from the first of May until at least next winter,
 -
by which time I trust the railway will be finished and completely equipped to run throughout the year.
In connection with the same railway, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say something further to my hon. friend the Minister oi Railways. Last year a request was made,- not by myself but by a big industrial enterprise in the county, the American Titanic Ore Company, the owners of a big mine,- for a branch line to be built nine miles north from Baie St. Paul to St. Urbain at a cost of $50,000 or $60,000, which would be a good feeder to this new railway. At the time the minister told me that a survey would be made and men would be sent to inquire about the possibilities of such a venture; but nothing has been done.
Another project has been brought before the Legislature of the Province of Quebec, and it is being supported by the people of my county and of the county of Chicoutimi, having in view pushing the same railway northward from Murray Bay to Chicoutimi. May I be permitted to say to the hon. Minister of Railways that I have not looked into this matter, but engineers of his department -men whom I know he holds in the greatest esteem-have told me that if this extension were made it would certainly bring a lot of business to the Quebec and Saguenay Railway, and the profitable traffic would be quite sufficient to pay the interest on the capital expenditure. I may add, Sir, that the projected extension would reduce the distance from Chicoutimi to Quebec by about forty-five or fifty miles. This district contains great lumber industries as well as manufactories of different kinds, so that such a line would at once get a great deal of traffic and at the same time act as a stimulus to local industry.
When the management decided last fall to take away the daily train service, I was assured by the Minister of Railways that the Government would sooner or later take over the entire railway and operate it as part of the Canadian National system. Later on I was told that this policy was not carried out on account of a certain little accident that happened on the railway. I have inquired from many people in my county if such an accident ever took place, and they have told me that this was not the ease, and they are most reliable people. While the engineers and contractors are still engaged in completing this railway I would urge upon the minister to come down and see that part of the country and meet the people, and I am sure that if he does so he will on his return take the necessary steps

to have these two branch lines immediatelj constructed.
The Minister of Railways towards the end of his speech pointed out that in a few years to come the Canadian National Railway system will in his opinion, he able to show a surplus. As the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) has well said this afternoon, there is freight in abundance everywhere in the province of Quebec, as well as in the other provinces, and the only thing the Government has to do is to go where the freight is available and so secure a good revenue. But, Mr. Speaker, I have one thing to object to in regard to the Canadian National Railway management-it is that men from the province of Ontario, such as Mackenzie and Mann, or, if they are not themselves in charge of affairs, their own agents and right bowers like Mr. D. D. Hanna and Mr. Mitchell, and others connected with them, are still in control of the system. I do not believe that people from other localities who are not at all conversant with the needs of a special district can themselves without personal inspection acquire a knowledge of its needs, and the president does not carry conviction by issuing orders from the province of Ontario or from the city of Ottwa and saying, "All goes well because I say so, and I am correct because I am paid a salary of $25,000 a year."
The minister has said that the rates charged by the Government railways were all light; that they might be increased a little later, but that they would be the same as those charged by other railways. I may be mistaken, but I have always thought that the rates changed by railway companies were fixed by the Railway Commission. Replying to a question which I put some time ago regarding the rates prevailing on the new railway in my county, the Minister of Railways informed me that these rates had been fixed by the officials of the Canadian National Railways. I am informed upon good authority that these fates are higher than the rates charged upon certain other railways for the carrying of goods over the same distances. For instance, $15.66 is charged for carrying fifty bags of cement which, carried over the same distance on other railways, would cost 10 cents per bag. Ten cents per 100 pounds was charged for one carload of hay shipped from Montreal to Quebec, a distance of 180 miles, whereas 14 cents per 100 pounds was charged for the same load from Quebec to Baie St. Paul, a distance of 60 miles. The charge for carrying a barrel of apples from
Quebec to Baie St. Paul is $1.70; I believe that is too high.
Last fall I took up with the Minister of Railways the matter of remedying the conditions existing through the lack of adequate railway facilities between Quebec and Murray Bay, and also the Railway Commission. I was informed by the Railway Commission at that time that they had no control over the railway operating between these points because the Government had not taken official charge of it. On the other hand, I was told by the minister a few days ago that the officials of the .Canadian National Railways had themselves fixed the rates charged on this railway. I would like to know what is the position in regard to this railway. One day we are told that the Government owns it, and then when we try to avail ourselves of that very fact and endeavour to have certain conditions remedied through their being brought before the proper board, we are told that the board has no jurisdiction.
The Minister of Railways spoke also about certain improvements made at Quebec and at certain other places. He said, for instance, that a huge sum of money had (been spent at Quebec and on the St. .Charles river. I was at the city of Quebec some time ago, and I do not believe that the Government have done all that they should have done at that place. As another hon. member dealt with this matter a few days ago I shall not go into it on this occasion, except to point out that this district seems to have been entirely neglected. Last autumn I was at Levis, right opposite Quebec, and I found that no station had been built there or even commenced. During the last five or six years the people of that place have only a kind of shack to serve as accommodation while waiting the arrival and departure of trains. I am told that there is a great need of repair on that part of the Canadian National Railways which is known as the Intercolonial. I travelled a good deal last year on the railway between Riviere Ouelle and Montreal; never in my life have I known the trains *[DOT]on that line to be on time.
I do not believe that the Government Railways can compete with the Canadian Pacific. The servants of the Government will always be the servants of the Government; we shall never be able to get from them the same service that is iendered by the employees of private concerns.
I wish to call attention also to the fact that there is no decent, safe and adequate station accommodation for those who use

the Canadian National Railways at the city of Quebec. I put a question on the Order Paper the other day inquiring of the minister whether the Government had considered the advisability of taking oyer the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix railway and linking it up with the Canadian National Railways, the old Canadian Northern, and with the Quebec and Saguenay. [DOT]He told me that this was still the'intention ,of the Government; I hope that it will be done as soon as possible. I was told that negotiations had been carried on for the acquisition of this railway, but for one reason and another it has not been acquired. It is not for me to dictate the policy of the Government, but here we have a condition where the Government operates a railway out of Quebec a certain distance, and from Quebec to St. Joachim, a distance of thirty miles on that line, they are not the owners of railway serving that district. So far the acquirement of part of this line Quebec and Saguenay was a good step, but the Government should do better and acquire the rest of the line in order that they may have a direct' line from Quebec to Murray Ray.
I directed the attention of the Government to the need for the building of stations along the line between Quebec and Murray Bay, and they said that they would [DOT]inquire into it. As is always the case when that reply is given, we heard no more about the matter. We are always told that the Board of Management of the Canadian National Railways will give attentive consideration to any representations made to it from different parts of the country. But I have found that it sometimes takes three or four months to get an answer to letters which I have sent to them concerning railway matters. I do not know how the system is run; whether there is a head office in Toronto, in Ottawa or in Quebec. But I do know that in Montreal there is a gentleman named Mr. Brady who represents the department and very often when I send him a communication I receive a reply to the effect that he will communicate with Ottawa or with Toronto; and I hear no more about it-that is the end of it.
I will not detain the House much longer; but in connection with the present policy of Government ownership of railways, I do not believe it is feasible or possible at present to bring under decent control and management all the different railways which the Government has acquired, unless absolutely right away, immediately, all the people from near and far who had anything

to do with the Canadian Northern railway before, are done away with. We heard that Mr. D. B. Hanna is the greatest railway man and exponent of railway problems.
I believe what the Government may say; but if up to date, Mr. Hanna had been so big and great as that, he certainly would have been retained by other big railways in the United States, as was the case with Mr. Gutelius who was manager and chief engineer of the Canadian Government railways previously. I do not really believe that the employees and the men who are at the head of this famous Canadian National Railway Company to-day are up to much, and we should immediately pay the best salaries possible, without looking at the amount, in order to get the most efficient men and the most efficient management.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: topic
subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Railways and Canals, chargeable to collection of revenue-Canadian Government railways, toward deficit of working expenditure for nine months ending December 31. 1920. the management of the railways being hereby authorized to apply the receipts and revenues toward payment of the working expenditure, $5,000,000.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Before we take up this Estimate, I should like to hsk a question of the minister. There is a statement made that on the 1st February, the number of Canadian freight cars in the United States was forty thousand odd and on the same date the number of United States freight cars in Canada was 24,000 odd, leaving a surplus of Canadian cars in the United States of 16,109. On the 1st March, the number of Canadian freight cars in the United States was 59,000 odd and the number of United States cars in Canada was 40,000 odd, leaving a surplus of Canadian freight cars in United States of 19,084. I understand that while the United States Government is giving back to the railways the control of their roads-the United States Car Service Commission continues to administer the service of freight cars until the 1st May. If that be true, it seems to me that the Canadian Government should be able to represent to the United States Government that we should have a fair reciprocity in freight cars. I am sure the minister will agree with me that it is

very necessary at this time that we should have cars to move Canadan products.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Everything that I personally or the Government or the railway companies could do to try to get our cars back, has been done. Through the British ambassador at Washington, we have urged the United States Government to give us back our cars; the Canadian Railway Association at Montreal have done everything that they could possibly do, and the heads of the different railways have been pressing the United States to return their cars. We have, however, so much to ship out that as fast as the United States railways return the cars, those cars are moved back into the United States and are retained there. There is a great shortage of cars in the United States at the present time, the railways in that country being short from 100,000 to 150,000 cars, and they will not let us have their cars. Nothing more could be done than has been done by the Government through the ambassador and by the railways acting through their organizations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I want to ask the minister a question in reference to a clause in the Grand Trunk Bill which was before the House last session and a clause which appears in the agreement between the Grand Trunk and the Government. At the last session of Parliament when the Bill was before the House, the following clause was in the Bill and was subsequently stricken out when the Bill was in committee:
The Government may lend to the said Committee of Management, upon the notes or other obligations of the Grand Trunk, such sums as the Government may from time to time deem necessary to the carrying on or operation of the Grand Trunk system.
Exception was taken to that clause on this side of the House, and the minister consented to its withdrawal. In the agreement there is a clause which is not in exactly the same words, but which seems to have very much the same purport, and it reads as follows:
The Managing Committee may. with the consent of the Governor in Council, borrow from the Government on Grand Trunk notes, or other obligations or securities approved of by the Governor in Council, for the carrying on of the operation or improvement of the Grand Trunk system.
In the opinion of the minister, is there any difference between these two clauses, and if so, what is the nature and extent of the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I am hardly in a position to give the hon. member an answer, because that is more of a financial question, and the Minister of Finance, if he were in his seat, could probably give a better answer than I could. As I understand the matter from reading this clause, that was intended to assist in financing the Grand Trunk railway, but the assistance is to be given only after the money is voted by Parliament. As I understand it, no money has been voted by Parliament for that purpose, and, therefore, no action has been taken up to the present time as regards giving any money to the Grand Trunk railway under that clause.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do I understand from the minister that under this clause in the agreement between the Government and the Grand Trunk, no money will be advanced to the Grand Trunk unless an appropriation is first made by Parliament for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is the way I understand the matter. Of course, I am speaking subject to correction pending discussion of the matter with the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I suppose we may refer to the matter again when the Minister of Finance is in the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

I want to call the minister's attention to the statement which he made when the hon. member for Chateau-guay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) raised the question about Canadian cars being held in the United States. If I understood the minister aright, he stated that the Canadian authorities had done everything possible to get those cars back, but that they had not succeeded. If a person, having got property legitimately at first, holds it against the owner's consent illegally and without the intention of returning it, he is subject to being accused of theft.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
But he is not holding it illegally. There is an international agreement that where a cay is on a foreign road, that road pays a per diem allowance for that car until it is returned to the original road that owned the car.
. The American railways are not holding those cars illegally, but it pays them to pay that per diem allowance rather than return our cars. The British Ambassador and Mr. Mahoney, who is connected with the Board of Commerce at Washington, are



making the strongest possible recommendations to get the ears back.
Is there any understanding between the British Ambassador of Washington and the American companies as to a limit within which these cars shall be returned?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No.

Would the minister be willing to place on the Table all the correspondence that has taken place between the British Ambassador and the other parties relative to the steps that have been taken to get back Canadian cars?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have no objection. The American Government has been urging the railways to return the cars, but the companies keep passing them from one road to another. No one road keeps the cars for a great length of time, but altogether they remain over there a long time. When they get the cars there they keep them. The. trend is more from Canada to the United States.
People want cars in this country, and the minister has to furnish them. If the minister could get back the Canadian cars on the other side, would that save any part of this item of $5,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No. We have another item providing for the purchase of new cars. If we got 14,000 cars back we would not require to order so many new ones. But the products of Canada must be got out. The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) was complaining because he could not get cars to take pulp-wood from the Transcontinental to the other side. If we allowed these oars to go over there, we would not get them back.

If the minister could get back these 14,000 cars it would effect a great saving to the Canadian people. Is there anything in the form of an agreement by which the Canadian people will be compensated for the holding of these cars on the other side?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: All we get is a per diem allowance, just as we have to pay a per diem allowance on American cars, but our railways get more revenue from this source on account of the adverse balance.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
The minister has just told the hon. member for Wright that the reason why the people of the Abitibi district are not supplied with cars to move their freight 
is because it is the deliberate policy of this Government not to supply cars that would go to the United States, because they would not get them back. Is that the policy of this Government in connection with all business in Canada, as regards grain, for instance? Let us follow the minister's statement to a conclusion. The hon. member for Pontiac this afternoon made the statement, supported by affidavit, that there were up in the Abitibi country 6,500 carloads of freight ready for the railway. The minister himself has told us that there are two ways of getting increased revenue for the railways; either by increased rates, or increased business. In this case the business is there. According to this statement, supported by affidavit, there are approximately 200 trainloads of freight waiting for transportation. The same condition exists all over the country. In Western Canada the grain is ready to be moved. Is it the deliberate policy of this Government not to supply cars for carrying wheat, oats, lumber, hay and other products of this country to the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No. Our policy is to serve Canada first; in other words, to look after interprovincial traffic. We require a certain number of cars for our own needs :n Canada, and if there is any surplus we use them for international traffic. What we have been urging the United States Government and the United States railways to do is to let their cars come over here and get this traffic. The hon. member will see that it is absolutely necessary to have a certain number of cars in Canada for our cwn business. If we were to act on his suggestion we would not have any cars in Canada at all.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: If you send these two hundred trainloads-	,

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Does the minister claim that all this traffic in the Abitibi district is intended for the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: If it is not, there is no trouble about cars. If we were to look after international trade, we would not have sufficient cars to take pulpwood, for instance, from some part in Canada to the mills where it is manufactured; we would not be able to take paper from Chicoutimi to Montreal. We have to protect first our own people in Canada, and use whatever surplus cars we have for international traffic.

The minister claims there is no trouble within Canada. Let me

tell him that cars shipped with wheat last November were not reported in Winnipeg on the main line of the Canadian Northern when I came down here on the 26th of February. In the period between November 1 and February 26 the cars had not arrived at Winnipeg, and that is the condition everywhere in the West. I pointed out to the minister the other day that of the few cars we had available in the Peace River country, 76 were standing on a side-track, of the Canadian National railways, for some three months and have never been moved in that time. I know that for a fact. Owing to the lack of cars we were unable to get out our grain. Some of us were lucky enough to secure cars last fall, but we were not able to get the grain transported even to the nearest point of inspection at Winnipeg. I know several cases of that kind. Furthermore, in the Edmonton district I have been unable to sell one bushel of grain since last fall for the simple reason that the elevators were, filled at threshing time, and they were unable to get cars to relieve the congestion. The elevators were still full at the time I left. I do not think that bears out altogether the statement of the minister that there is no trouble at all if the cars are not going to the United States. The trouble is on the main line, and the minister can very easily obtain information on the matter. We have had no markets along the line of the Canadian Northern in Alberta because the elevators have been filled and cars have not been available to relieve the congestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is the first complaint I have heard this winter with reference to the operation of this railway. There may be other complaints, but they have not reached me.
The primary cause of the trouble was that the elevators were filled at threshing time and transports could not be obtained to relieve the congestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The hon. member will see that the congestion begins at the seaports-Halifax, St. John, Portland or New York-and keeps backing up, with the result that the elevators are filled. It must be obvious that we could not supply cars to be used fpr storage purposes.
I was answering the point made by the minister that there was no trouble except one of an international character.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The point I wish to emphasize is that' there is a great quantity of produce that has to be moved backwards and forwards between the provinces, and we try to protect that traffic first by having sufficient cars to move it.

Probably the reason why the minister has not received more complaints is the statement of the railway authorities that they could not give cars to relieve the congestion owing to the feed shortage in the South, which called for the use of cars for transporting feed thither from the North. We accepted that statement, considering that, in view of the seriousness of the situation, it was perhaps only right that the live stock should be saved.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Before six o'clock I want to put a question on record. What is the per diem rental charge on cars between different routes? How long is the contract made for, and when does it expire? Further, is the rental based on an estimate sufficiently high to cover reasonable interest on investment?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Ninety cents a day is charged on each side forty-eight hours after the car has arrived, and that is unlimited. We cannot force a car back.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Is this arrangement from year to year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The rates are revised from time to time.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the Committee rose at six o'clock we were considering item No. 335, a vote of $5,000,000 for the Canadian Government railways'. Shall the item carry?

The minister stated before six o'clock that the Government had done everything in their power to get cars returned from the United States. About a year ago I brought this question up in the House, and the Government then promised that they would undertake to make some arrangement whereby these Canadian cars would be brought back from the other side of the line. During the past year the United States Government had control of all the railways in that country, and I would like to know if there has been any attempt on the part of this Govern-

ment to arrive at an understanding with them-an understanding between the two Governments rather than between individual railway companies-as to an exchange of these cars, and whether the Canadian Government will take the responsibility of seeing to it that Canadian cars shall be returned to this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman was not in the Chamber before six o'clock when I made a statement on this matter. The Canadian Government communicated with the British Ambassador at Washington with a view to his taking the matter up, and he is doing all that he possibly could. In addition to that we have a representative of the Board of Commerce in Washington who has been endeavouring to arrange the matter with the railway organization at the United States capital. Likewise, our railway association at Montreal, together with President Beatty of the Canadian Pacific railway, and President Hanna of the Canadian National Railway system, have been using every effort to bring about, an improvement of the existing conditions, to say nothing of messages which the Minister of Railways and other departments have been forwarding. I promised to get all the correspondence and lay it on the Table. The Deputy Minister of Railways has already received instructions to obtain all the information available in order to show what efforts have been made to get the cars owned by Canadian railway companies back into Canada.

Seeing that we have 4,000 cars in the United States, is it not possible to have the per diem allowance increased, and have it not only doubled, but trebled? The cost of cars has increased three or four (times over what it was a few years ago, and surely there ought to be some way of making the allowance for these cars three or four times more than it is to-day. The nominal sum that is at present charged is a snap for the United States companies that are using our cars; but if the allowance were increased three or four times it would in all probability produce better results.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The per diem charge was formerly sixty cents and it was increased to ninety cents.
That is of no avail.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: I would suggest $2 or $3 a day.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
In that case how would you collect the amount from the companies over there? They have the cars and we cannot get them back until they are prepared to return them. For our railway companies to start quarrelling with a company on the other side would, I am afraid, result in complications that would not be to our advantage in the long run. I think I am quite safe in saying that the (Canadian Pacific, the National railways, and the Grand Trunk, are all just as anxious as they can be to get the cars back, and they are making every exertion to do so. The fact of the matter is that the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National railways are compelled to buy more oars because of the shortage in Canada caused by Canadian cars being in the United States. The Government and the Canadian railway companies are doing all they can, and I do not think that any further effort can be made beyond what is being resorted to up to the. present time.
Mr. J. E. ARMiSTRONG: This matter has been going on for several years. The sum of sixty, or even ninety cents, per diem, is such a small amount in comparison with the capital invested in a car that the authorities on the other side of the international boundary line should not be annoyed if they are charged $2 or $3 per diem in respect of cars that are not returned. With such an allowance as that Canadian railway companies would be in a position to possibly pay the interest on the cost of building cars in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
In that case the United States railways might say: We will not exchange cars; if you are going to charge that rate we will not tranship your cars on our road. Suppose a dozen cars arrived at Niagara Falls, New York, and we said to the American company: The per diem charge for those cars is $3 or $4 a day; they would simply say: If you do not want to comply with the rules in the United States we will not take your cars. In that case what could we do?
Mr. J. E. ARMiSTRONG: Is the minister taking up with the American authorities the question of increasing the allowance to $2 or $3?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The railway companies themselves have taken it up and we have discussed every phase of the matter with them in the hope of getting the cars back. It is

the interest of the railways and. the public that guides us as to what is best to do.
, Mr. BELAND: This is a very serious question indeed. The trade figures show that Canada has imported in the past year about $300,000,000 worth more than it exported. That would in itself .indicate that there should be many more ears in Canada from the United States than there are Canadian cars in the adjoining republic. May I ask the .minister whether it has not been the policy of the Canadian railway companies, or of the 'Government National railways, to hold in Canada as many cars coming from the United States as possible in view of the fact that United States companies weTe retaining Canadian cars on the other side? In view of the trade figures I cannot understand why we should have fewer American cars on this side than they have of Canadian cars in the country to the South.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
will realize that it takes more cars to carry Canadian products such as pulp, and lumber, which are bulky in their character, to the other side.
But we import coal; we imported $40,000,000 worth. Then there are automobiles.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We are not holding any more cars to-day than are required for our own trade. However, this is a very important question and if hon. gentlemen agree I would like to have a day set apart for its discussion by the Railway Committee. If satisfactory to hon. gentlemen, I will arrange to have the railway representatives there to explain the situation and also present such information as can be got from the Railway Department. I can only repeat that the Government and the railway companies are making every possible effort to get our cars back, and we cannot put forth any more exertions than we are already doing to bring about that result.

I do not wish to controvert the minister's statement. I think the Canadian National railways, the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk have tried all they can to get their cars back to Canada. However, can we not say of the Canadian National railways that they have been more lenient than American companies in that they have allowed American cars to go back to the United iStatets whilst their Own Canadian cars were retained in that country?	i '

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: What the hon. gentleman means is that we should hold more American cars in this country?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: How are we going to ship pulp-wood to the United States if that is done? The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) has complained about pulp-wood along the Transcontinental railway remaining unshipped. We must send the cars back to the United States."

You must reverse the situation. How can the Americans ship large quantities of goods to Canada unless they have the cars? Because the minister must remember, they export to this country $300,000,000 more than we export to them. And these goods are not in the shape of diamonds or gold rings, which require but, a small amount of car space. For instance, besides coal we import $40,000,000 of automobiles, and $30,000,000 of machinery, traction engines, etc. This freight requires spacious cars.

I would like to know if the minister is prepared to answer the question that I put this afternoon but which was ruled out of order at that time; that is,, with respect to the extension of the Canadian Northern from Bruderheim to Whit-ford, Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: My deputy tells me that we have no item in the Estimates for that work so far this year. However, the matter does not arise under this item, and before the item passes I will obtain more information. I have a memorandum before me and we will ascertain from the management of the Canadian National railways in Toronto if any further information is available. The hon. gentleman stated this afternoon that I made a promise at the meeting of the Railway Committee. It is hard to keep all these matters in recollection, but whatever promise I made would be on the strength of information given by the officials of the Railway Department at that particular time. I shall draw their attention to the statement now made by the hon. gentleman and before the item passes will endeavour to obtain whatever supplementary information is necessary.	*

My reason for pressing the question at this time is in view of the promise which was made. A delegation from the district was here at the time and the matter was fully discussed in the Rail-

iway Committee. The people of the district have been looking forward to the department making good that promise that was made, and I was asked to bring the question up and remind the minister of it. The people of that part of Alberta expect to get some definite information as to whether they may expect to get the railway extended into that section this year. The minister says there is no item. Am I to conclude from his statement that nothing is going to be done with the road this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Before giving a positive answer I would like to have an opportunity of further consultation with the management to see if I have overlooked it in their statement. I will give my hon. friend an answer .later on,

Before we get away from the question of car exchange I want to ask , *the Government if they have any policy in regard to the exchange of cars between the United'States and Canada. A few years ago we sent a deputation to Washington to negotiate a treaty, not through the British Ambassador, but directly on behalf of Canada. Is it not possible to negotiate another treaty with regard to the exchange of cars? There is rib question that this car shortage is going to continue, for we must export goods to the United States until at least we have balanced the trade situation. If the Government is not in a position to negotiate with the American Government, we must expect a continuance of the same confusion. The people I spoke of this afternoon, in the Abitibi district, will get no relief until this -situation is cleaned up, and if they are not going to obtain relief they might, as well know it and get out of the country.
There can be no question about the United States Government legislating so that arrangements may be made to get these cars back, and, of course, the Dominion Government has the same power to legislate for the return of American cars from this side. The minister points out that if you make the per diem charges $4 or $5 the American roads will not accept the cars. But there is no necessity to make that charge apply at once; it can be arranged to become effective after a certain lapse of time. But. there must be some arrangement whereby Canadian and American roads will exchange cars on a .more satisfactory basis than obtains today. It is not for the Railway Committee to negotiate between several hundred lines in the United States and in Canada; it is a question to be settled between the two Governments. I pointed that out last year, but 
apparently the old condition of affairs still exists. The minister says: Let this question be settled by the Railway Committee. It is not a question for the Railway Committee to settle; it is a question for the Government of B this country to negotiate with the Government of the United States to see if they cannot come to some arrangement whereby a settlement can be reached.

I see that the item is:
Canadian Government Railways, toward deficit of working expenditure for nine months ending December 31, 1920.
That is next year. May I ask the minister what that working expenditure is based upon? I understand that this year we are having a deficit of $30,000,000, and from the newspapers I find glowing accounts of the progress our railway system is making, and the hopes entertained that our railway revenues will lift the entire burden of taxation from the shoulders of our taxpayers. Of course, I quite appreciate that the minister cannot answer every question of detail which may be put to him, but on the other hand these are supposed to ibe Government railways, and still more are they supposed .to be Parliament railways. The Government do not hear as much about bad operation of any of their railways as the individual member of Parliament through whose riding the railway runs, and the only case where the member can put his grievance before the authorities is here. Therefore I think that a field day in the Railway Committee will not amount to much, because we will merely get very glowing accounts from Mr. Hanna and the other officials-I do not blame them -to assure the people that their railways are being operated efficiently and to encourage their patronage. First of all, I want to know what to-day constitutes the Canadian Government Railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Canadian Northern system, the Intercolonial railway and the Transcontinental Tailway. Answering the other question, how I arrived at that $5,000,000, the loss for the past fiscal year ending March 31, was $7,500,000. Now we are bringing the Transcontinental and the Intercolonial fiscal year to an end on December 31 the same as the fiscal year of the Canadian Northern and all other railways. So we estimate $5,000,000 as being the deficit for the year.	,

While I am on my feet, Mr. Chairman. The other day I put some questions to the Minister of Railways- very simple questions that could have been answered yes or no, or very shortly. The

minister, as was his right, moved for a return. I got the return to-day. I am not going to deal with it in detail, but I will merely state the questions I put. They were:
Has an Order in Council been passed entrusting the said company-I was talking about the Canadian National Railway Company- with the management and operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific and Intercolonial railways?
The answer is no. The second question I put was:
If so, what is the date of the Order in Council ?
Naturally, there is no date. No Order in Council was passed. Then I put this other question:
If an Order in Council was not passed, why was such an Order in Council not passed?
There is no answer. I have this to complain of, Mr. Chairman. You can sue the Canadian Northern railway before the courts of your province and bring the case to trial; but if you try to sue the Transcontinental you find that it will take you a year to get a fiat-and I am speaking from experience. I understand the situation perfectly well. The Secretary of State sends the petition to the Minister of Justice; the Minister of Justice cannot pass on the facts unless he has them before him; therefore he sends the petition back to the Minister of Railways; the Minister of Railways sends it to Toronto, and those in authority in Toronto sends it down to Leduc or to some other headquarters of the Transcontinental, where they ask a man who knows something about lumber to cruise certain territory which has been burnt by the railway and make a report; the man makes his report, sometimes it is unsatisfactory, and a second report is called for; the report goes to Toronto, from Toronto it is sent to the Minister of Railways, and he sends it to the Department of Justice. In two instances, I do not know whether the reports were lost or what happened, but the cases did not go any further. I know of a case where the petition of right was served in July and the report was made in the following February. The cruisers went through the bush in February where the fire took place the preceding June. I admit the winter season is a better time for tramping through the bush on snowshoes and traversing the frozen lakes and rivers, but in my experience up the St. Maurice river I never heard of a cruiser going out during the winter, especially when the snow is high, to see what damage had been done by fire. '
I want to find out why the Transcontinental railway is not put in the same position as the Canadian Northern Railway system so that a man who suffers damage from negligence or any other cause whatever can go before a tribunal in the locality where the damage was caused and where all the witnesses live and have his case tried the same as if he was bringing an action against the Canadian Northern railway which is also a government railway. The Government has no more interest in the one railway than in the other, and I do not see what reason they can have for putting a litigant to all the trouble of waiting five, six or seven months before getting a fiat to bring his case before the Exchequer Court.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The reason is that the Canadian Northern railway is an incorporated private company, of which we are the stockholders. The hon. member will remember that we passed a Bill in a previous session whereby we are going to transfer them all
Yes, I well remember you passed it by the use of the closure.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
That is the reason it was such a good Bill.
The intention is to transfer all these railways to the Canadian National Railway Company, and then, of course, if there should be considered cause for action against the Transcontinental, such action could be brought just as can now be done in the case of the Canadian Northern. The hon. member is right in saying that every facility should be afforded to those who have just cause for action against the Government railway. Possibly there may have been delay in the case referred to; if the matter had been brought to my attention we would have facilitated the proceedings in every possible way. The delay in connection with the Grand Trunk acquisition has prevented us from taking the necessary steps to bring these lines under the Canadian National Railway' Company, but ultimately the Canadian Northern, the Transcontinental and the Intercolonial will all be subject to the one law so far as the bringing of action against them is concerned.

I do not think that the minister expects me to take that as an answer or as a reason for the course that has been followed. The object of the incorporation of the Canadian National Railway Company was to put under one system of

operation and make subject to one law all the railways operated by the Canadian Government. Now, here is an anomaly; an Act is passed for the special purpose of bringing under one management the Transcontinental and the Intercolonial; yet neither of them is brought under that management. To say that you are waiting for the Grand Trunk is no excuse; you might as well say that you are waiting for the Chaudiere Falls Railway or for the St. Maurice Valley Railway. I do not want to be understood as criticizing the department, because I understand the difficulty that is encountered when reports pertaining to such matters as this have to go from the Secretary of State to the Minister of Justice, from the Minister of Justice to the Minister of Railways, from the Minister of Railways to the Toronto office, or to Moncton in the case of the Intercolonial, and so on. I simply want to point out how unfair it is >
to the man who suffers damages alleged to have been caused by a Government railway when he has to deal with two Government railways, one operated by the Canadian National Railway Company and the other not so operated, although it should naturally form part of the Canadian National system. It is true that the letters " C.N.R. " still appear on the sieves of the cars forming part of the equipment of the Canadian National Railway System; but let that pass. If we are going to have operation of Government railways by an incorporated company, let us have it for the whole system, including the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental. Great damage was caused in the St. Maurice region last year through the alleged negligence-as to that the courts will decide-of the Transcontinental; millions of feet of timber were burned because of that negligence. While on this question of operation let me refer to a condition which exists on the Canadian Northern line between Montreal and Quebec at a place called Glenada, where there is no agent. The next station is Grand'Mere; at that point there is an agent. As I came upon the train to-day it was directed to my attention that an unsatisfactory state of affairs prevails at this point. Ste. Flore, with a population of 3,000 people, is at the door of Grand'Mere, and the nearest point from which they can ship their freight is Glenada, but as there is no agent at Glenada, they have to ship to and from Grand 'Mere. But the Canadian Pacific station at Grand'Mere is on the level, and the Canadian Northern station is at the foot of the hill. If a man has to order a car of freight, 
instead of having it shipped on the Canadian Northern he gets it by Canadian Pacific in order to avoid the haul up the hill. If we had an agent at Glenada, we would get all that traffic and prevent it from being diverted to the Canadian Pacific. These things ought to be inquired into. I was told to-day that carload after carload of freight was being lost to the Canadian Government Railways because of our having no agent at Glenada.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I shall see that the attention of the management is drawn to my hon. friend's statement.

The minister told us this afternoon that the loss on operating expenses is $14,000,000 and interest charges $19,000,000, making a total deficit of $33,000,000. What have these roads cost the country by way of deficits during 1919? By deficits, I mean outgo less income. What I want to get at is this: The Government had adopted the policy of Government ownership of railways. Having regard t& the fact that in past years we have put up large sums of money for the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and so on, will the minister say whether the present state of affairs is less costly to the people than the system previously followed?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
want the gross earnings?
Mr. .PARDEE: I want to know how the loss on Government operations compares with the result from private operations prior to 1919.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: My hon. friend has the figures correctly. The loss on operating expenses was $14,000,000; the fixed charges on the Canadian Northern about $19,000,000. I mentioned also in my statement this afternoon that the loss on the Grand Trunk Pacific, which is not a part of the Canadian National railway system, was $5,000,000, to which should be added $8,800,000 for fixed charges, making a total of $14,000,000 on the Grand Trunk Pacific.
That is, $14,000,000 must be added to the $33,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes; that includes the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Transcontinetal, the Intercolonial and the Canadian Northern. I gave all the figures this afternoon.
What was the total cost to the people of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The loss was $47,000,000 during the past year.
Does that include maintenance?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, and includes also
some $8,800,000 of fixed charges on the iGrand Trunk Pacific and $19,000,000 of fixed charges on the Canadian Northern.

So that the people of
Canada paid out during 1919 on account of the public ownership of railways, maintenance included, $47,000,000. Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
No, that is hardly a
fair way to put it. Of course, during 1919-

Put it, " for the luxury
of operating railways."

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: During 1919 the cost of operation of the Government Railways was increased by $19,000,000 for wages alone, and there were no increases given. Therefore, it is not fair to compare 1919 with the previous year, because in 1918 some increases in rates were granted. But if we take the situation as the hon, member has stated it, he is correct; those railways lost $47,000,000 last year.
Is that the total loss?

I do not think the minister is putting the case strongly enough, because we are face to face with another rise in freight rates. It is not more than a year or two ago since the first increase in freight rates was made. I think there was an increase of five per cent in 1916, a second increase of fifteen per cent, and later on a further increase of twenty-five per cent. My recollection is that the rates have increased forty-five per cent already, and it looks as if we shall have another increase in order to meet the deficit. Therefore, public ownership is going to give us a deficit of $47,000,000 which the ratepayers of this country will have to shoulder, and in addition to that we are face to face with an increase in rates which will also be a burden on the people of Canada. I would advise the minister to increase the rates so that those people who are shouting for public ownership will understand what it really means, because they will have to pay for it. I do not see why the ordinary taxpayers of this country should be called upon to pay deficits incurred in the running of our railroads. The people who use the railways should pay for the railways. "Why should a man who lives twenty, thirty, forty or sixty miles from a railway,' as is the case with many people in my constituency, have to
pay for accommodation received by people in the larger places? It is not fair that this large deficit should be levied upon the general taxpayers of the country. The railways should bear their own burden, the rates should be put up in order that the bills may be paid. And after a while people will find out what public ownership is. Public ownership has been a failure in the United States; it has been a failure in Great Britain; it is a failure in Canada; and the sooner we come to learn the lesson, the better.
There is another matter which I want to bring to the attention of the minister and it is this. I listened carefully to his statement this afternoon, but I have no clear idea as to how we stand on this railway question. I suppose the minister has; but it will be necessary for him to prepare a statement such as is prepared by a joint stock company at the end of the year, showing his assets and liabilities, and his profit and loss account, and give it to the members of this House, so that we may know where we stand. The minister says that he has a deficit of $47,000,000, but that does not give us any information. Wo want to know where that money has gone; we want to know what assets we have, and the only way in which that can be put before us is by a regular statement like that prepared by a joint stock company. If the president of a joint stock company were to come before his shareholders with a story like the one the minister told us to-day and say that he had operated the business for a year and had a deficit of some $47,000,000, why, he would not be elected again, I am quite sure of that.
Neither will Union Government.

The minister must give a summary, of course; but when he gives us a regular bookkeeping statement-, showing his assets and liabilities and his profit and loss account, we shall be able to judge for ourselves. As the matter stands to-day we are not able to understand him.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The hon. member will probably find all that he has asked for in the statements that I did not read out today, but that will appear in Hansard. If he does not, I shall be glad to furnish any further information that may be required. With reference to public ownership, the Intercolonial railway, which is publicly owned, lost $7,500,000 last year in operation. Does the hon. member want to suggest that that road should be handed over

~ to a private corporation on account of its losing $7,500,000? The Canadian Northern lost only some $6,000,000 in the operation of .its whole system, whereas the Intercolonial lost $7,500,000 in addition to the interest on a capital of $125,000,000. What private corporation could we hand the Intercolonial over to now? The Grand Trunk Pacific was handed over to us; we could not help taking it over; what could we do with it? We could not close it down; no private corporation would take it off our hands, and we are compelled to operate it. When it was built we were responsible for it; we guaranteed the bonds. Therefore, it is impossible to hand back the roads that are really losing the most. No private corporation wants the Grand Trunk Pacific, and I do not think the people in the Lower Provinces would agree to handing over the Intercolonial to a private corporation even though it has lost $7,500,000 plus the interest on the capital. For myself, I would not want to hand it over; it was built to connect the Eastern Provinces with the Western Provinces, and I want it kept In the name of the people of Canada.

The minister need not try to frighten me with the Intercolonial because I have no doubt that if the Intercolonial were put into the hands of a private company, it would do better than it is doing to-day. The Intercolonial was one of the bargains entered into at Confederation; it was one of the terms on whidh the Maritime Provinces came into this union. If the Maritime Provinces desire to keep the Intercolonial as a government owned road and to compel the Dominion of Canada to live up to its bargain, I will not object to that; but no enterprise of this kind pays and it is impossible to make it pay under Government ownership, because it is inherent in the management of railways that men have to act quickly; they have some times to take chances; they have to conduct business in a way that it is not suitable for a Government to do. The Intercolonial has not always paid in the past; but I know a few occasions when it did pay under good management, and it should have paid better during later years than it has done. I do not know that I can point out the reasons why it has not paid, but the minister ought to know why it has not paid better than it has.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The reason last year was on account of the increase in wages, which added a large amount to the deficit; and during the war the increased cost of
[;Mr. Sinclair.]
operation was on account of the increase in wages and rates were not advanced in a corresponding ratio.

I understand that the rates in Eastern Canada are higher than those in Western Canada. If I remember aright, when the rates were raised in 1916, the increase applied only to districts east of Port Arthur; the rates in Western Canada remaining the same. If it be true that the eastern section of the railway is on a higher scale than the western section, that is a reason why the minister ought to have made the eastern section pay better than it has paid. I have no doubt whatever that the money has been wasted. The minister has not told us that a profit and loss account would appear in Hansard. If it does, we shall be able to examine it to-morrow morning; but if there is not a straight bookkeeping account for us to examine, the minister should not ask us to pass this item until he submits a statement of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will find the information on Hansard. If not, of course, I will give him any information he wishes. The hon. member, I think, stated that the Canadian Pacific Railway gave a statement of their earnings weekly. The Canadian National Railways have been doing the same thing. Their earnings are published in the trade papers. The Canadian Pacific, I believe, send a card showing their earnings to all their shareholders.

What amount was paid
out of earnings on account of maintenance and upkeep?
* Mr. J. D. REID: According to the statement I submitted, the operating expenses were $60,034,018.
i Mr. CAHILL: That is not what I want. According to the minister's statement, the deficit on account of interest charges and operating expenses amounted to $47,000,000. Now if there is a deficit in operation you could not, of course, take any money out of earnings and put it into maintenance of way or upkeep.
. Mr. J. D. REID:	If the hon. member
wants the items under the heading of Maintenance alone, I cannot give him those figures this evening.

Let me put my question in another way. There is such a thing as the maintenance of'way of railways. The roadbed has to be kept up to a certain

standard; new ties, new rails and fittings have to be put in. In the statement of the Canadian Pacific, for instance, I find that for the year 1918 they paid on account of maintenance of way, new structures, and so on, $28,000,000, and on maintenance and equipment $22,000,000, making a total of $50,000,000 spent out of earnings. After deducting this amount from their net receipts, there is a surplus of. $24,000,000. The receipts are not considered as earned until they have maintained the road in an efficient condition. The minister stated this afternoon that 78 per cent, I think, of the receipts on the Government railways was paid out in wages. The railways must also consume coal, for instance, and if 78 per cent of the receipts was paid out in wages there would be very little left for maintenance of way. What I want is a bookkeeping account, to show where this money that was received went to.
, Mr. J. D. REID: I would ask my hon. friend to let his question stand, and I will get the details a little more fully.

I am quite willing to do
that provided the minister will report progress.

The minister ought to
know under what heading maintenance expenses are charged. Are they charged to capital or to operation? Such items as maintaining the roadbed, for instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Any expenses in connection with renewing or repairing the old roadbed would be charged to operation, not to capital.

Were such expenses
charged to operation in 1919?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes. Those expenses
,are charged to operation before we get the net receipts.

Referring to the question
of maintenance, I should like to supplement the statement made bj the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) a short time ago. He stated that on the Canadian National between Montreal and Quebec there weie stations without agents.
And agents without stations.

More than that, there are stopping places, which should be stations, where absolutely no shelter for freight or passengers is provided. In the county of Joliette, for instance, there is a stopping place called St. Pierre, which is situated
in a very densely populated section. There is no shelter of any kind there, and up to last fall there was no road provided by the Government to the place where the train stops. I have been corresponding with Mr. Hanna in regard to this particular place for about a year, but have had no success whatever. I would ask the minister to see that some shelter is provided for the public in places so thickly populated as the county of Joliette and at such stopping places as St. Pierre, which is about nine miles from the city of Joliette. How can human beings, be expected to stand out in a field, in the open, at all seasons of the year, and especially in the winter months when the temperature is sometimes thirty below zero, waiting for the Government train-and unfortunately these trains are very often late? We are all aware that the trains of the Canadian National between Montreal and Quebec are running late most of the time, especially in winter, and you can easily imagine the plight of these people standing out there in an exposed place without shelter. I hope this will strike the minister as being a proper and a reasonable representation to make, and I should like him to give me the assurance now that something will be done to remedy the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I shall bring this matter to the attention of the management. Of course, I have not the power to order the erection of shelters wherever they are asked for, I can only lay the matter before the management. I am sure, however, they will consider cases of this kind favourably provided financial conditions warrant the expenditure. I think from what I have learnt from hon. members and the public generally that there has been a great improvement during the past year along the whole system. The management are doing all they can to remedy as quickly as possible conditions such as my hon. friend has mentioned.
So are we.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This afternoon the minister commented rather favourably on the widening of the gauge of the Prince Edward Island Railway between Charlottetown and Summerside. I should like to ask if it is the intention to proceed with the widening of the gauge over the entire system.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
We shall not proceed with that work during the present year. By standardizing the gauge between Char-

lottetown and Summerside we can take care of about 75 per cent of the trade of Prince JSdward Island. As soon as financial conditions will permit standardizing the gauge of the rest of the railway on Prince Edward Island that work will be proceeded with, but not this year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is an expense that is inevitable, and there would seem to be very little ground for not proceeding with it now":	At present 25 per
cent of the Island is without the accommodation it should have. That means a double shipment of all freight carried over the narrow gauge. I would strongly urge the minister to reconsider the matter and see if it not possible to proceed with the widening of the gauge
over the entire system.
/

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I am afraid we cannot consider this proposal this year. The other parts of the island have the narrow gauge system, and the only inconvenience is involved where there is trans-shipment. This, however, is not so serious because it is done by the railway officials at Charlottetown and Summerside. The widening that has been so far done is of great advantage, and I quite appreciate the necessity for completing the work over the whole system as soon as possible. But financial conditions, we felt, would not justify our doing it during the present year. Now, Mr. Chairman, as I have an important appointment which I should like to keep, and as the Minister of Naval Service (Mr. Ballantyne) is prepared to go on with his Estimates, I should be glad if the Committee would pass this item.
No, no.
We can Teport progress, and the minister may leave.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I move that further consideration of the item be postponed.
Item stands.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amount required for the construction of vessels in accordance with Government programme, $20,000,000.
May I ask the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) to remain during the discussion. We found him so useful to us on the last occasion that we would appreciate h:s advice again.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I should like to refer again to the law of the country 
and the way in .which these contracts have been awarded, but I desire to do so in the presence of the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster), because I think the matter is important enough to call for a statement from the leader of the Government himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think I can satisfy the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), as well as other hon. members in this matter. I fully explained the other evening the reasons why we let the contracts in the way in which we did; and with particular reference to the legal phase of the question, I showed that where an emergency exists the Government are justified in placing contracts in the way they did in connection with our shipbuilding programme. I am sure hon. members will agree that there was a two-fold emergency. In the first place, the war was on and the Government were anxious to get the ships; secondly, we were exceedingly desirous to keep men employed in the various yards from Halifax to Prince Rupert. I announced the other night that the Government shipbuilding programme was at an end, and in connection with any further contracts that may he let we shall follow the law and call for public tenders, as no emergency now exists. I am quite sure that this explanation will satisfy my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This item involves a sum of $20,000,000 which is a very large sum, and I would ask the minister if it is not possible, in connection with any portion of this amount, to call for tenders for the work that is to he done. Twenty million dollars is a big proportion of the total estimates for public works, and I might point out to my hon. friend that the total expenditure on this single matter is something like $70,000,000, an amount equal to the total expenditure of Canada only a few years ago. That all of this work should be done without tenders being called for in connection with a single contract, when the statute expressly provides that no contract exceeding $5,000 in amount shall be awarded unless public tenders are called for, seems to be a serious violation of the law of the land and one which even the minister himself will' find it difficult to justiffy.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I was under the impression that I had fully covered the ground the other night, but I shall be glad to do so again. As I said a moment or two ago, the war was in progress and Canada wanted ships Ibadly, and to have called for public tenders at that time would have meant

that two or three yards might perhaps have quoted at a lower rate than the other yards throughout the country; and if the Government had placed an order with, say, three yards that had only six berths, there would have been a serious delay in getting the ships. Furthermore, there was the labour situation to be considered. After all, however, the paramount question is this: Has the public interest been as fully safeguarded by the system which the Government adopted during the war and the reconstruction period as if public tenders had been called for? I take it that this is the question which the leader of the Opposition has in mind. I assume that he desires to be assured, and to have the public assured, that these ships were ordered at as low prices as if public tenders had been called for. Well, let me assure the hon. gentleman as well as other (members of the House that no lower prices could have been obtained had public tenders been called for in the usual way. Indeed, I will go further, and say that these ships were ordered at lower prices than if tenders had been called for. Hon. members who come from cities where shipbuilding yards are located know full well that I did not accept the first price that was quoted me by any of the shipyards. I had prices checked up as to cost, and exercised all the business ability of which I am possessed, whatever it may be worth, as well as the lability of the technical officers who were associated with me, in order that we might reduce the prices to, as low a point as possible. I made as close a bargain for the people a,s I possibly could, and I am thoroughly satisfied as a responsible minister that these ships have been orderd at lower prices than if public tenders had been called for. I have fully explained the reason for the deviation from the law. The emergency existed; it was imperative that the ships should be turned out; we were in a hurry for them; and if I had followed the advice which has been preferred by the leader of the Opposition the Government would not have to-day thirty ships in commission. Byfollowing the system which we adopted we got the ships in half the time that would have otherwise been required. Furthermore, the yards employed 25,000 men, and we wanted to distribute the contracts evenly amongst all the yards throughout the country. I am sure that hon. members will agree that the emergency, and the war conditions that existed at the time, as well as the desirability of giving employment to all of these 25,000 men, most of whom
are returned soldiers, justified the Government in seeing to it that the shipbuilding programme was evenly apportioned. I have no regrets as to the manner in which the contracts were placed.
