I think they were placed properly in the public interest. Our programme, as I stated the other night is now finished. Any further orders that the Government may have to give will certainly be awarded in accordance with the law, and after public tender. I am quite satisfied to do that, I wish to follow no other policy. The law is there, and if there is no emergency I must follow the law. The Government must also observe that course. I am thoroughly satisfied that if we were ordering more ships and do so by public contract, the people of this country would pay more for those ships than was the case under the system of ordering which the Government adopted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I realize that no good purpose can be served in a discussion of what was done during the period of the war. The war is made to cover a multitude of sins, and so far as the Government's violation of the law of the land in awarding these contracts is concerned, I iam quite prepared to allow the minister to use the war as an excuse as regards any emergency that may have existed at that time. But the war has now been over for sixteen months, and I am not sure from the minister's statement that contracts have not been awarded since that time. The point I am particularly anxious to make at the moment is, that we are asked now to vote another $20,000,000 not for any expenditure to be incurred as the result of an emergency, but for expenditures to be incurred during the coming year. I would therefore like to know from the minister if it is not possible, with respect to any part of this $20,000,000, to follow the law as regards the inviting of tenders for the work to be done under that expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In answer to the leader of the Opposition I might frankly state that all contracts have been placed subject to Parliament voting this amount of money. The urgency existed to keep our returned soldiers employed, and the Government are anxious to get the ships just as quickly as they possibly can; so all the contracts have been placed. I mentioned the figures involved the other night and perhaps I had better state them again. The total payments up to April, 1919, amounted to $19,510,322.35. The total payments from April, 1919, to March 1, 1920,

amounted to $24,194,639.78. The total payments on account of the Government's (Shipbuilding programme amount to $43,704,962.13. The balance available on March 1 from the vote for the current year amounts to $15,505,361.22. In addition to this balance that is available, the Government are now asking for another vote of $20,000,000, part of which is a re-vote from last year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have noticed a reference that my hon. friend has made to the conditions under which these contracts have been awarded, that they are subject to Parliament voting the amount. That is what we are doing at the present moment. What I would like to ask the minister, while we are voting this amount, is, can we not in some way incorporate the condition that the amount shall be voted and expended in accordance with the provisions of the law of the land? Let me read from the statutes of 1906, part 2, chapter 39, the section which governs this matter:
"Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department oi the Government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works, except in cases:
(a)	of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest; or,
(b)	in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department; or
(c)	where the estimated cost of the work is less than five thousand dollars and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
Now the amount in this case is not less than $5,000, it is $20,000,000. That being so, I am asking the minister: Is it not possible-if not in regard to the whole of the $20,000,000, at least in regard to some part of it-to invite tenders in accordance with the provisions of the statute which I have quoted?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can only answer to the leader of the Opposition that these contracts were placed quite some months ago, with the exception of one or two on the Pacific coast which latter that we were holding up because the department ovei which I preside and the ship-builders otit there could not agree on the cost of changing from coal-burning to oil-burning. Aside from that, however, the contracts were placed some months ago, and there are no further contracts now to be awarded.
Are we to understand that the contracts were awarded before the money was voted by Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member
probably heard my statement a few moments' ago that there was still a balance available on Marcti 1 of $15,505,361.22, which has not yet been expended. In addition to that we are now asking for a vote of $20,000,000, part of which is a re-vote from last year. The hon. member will therefore see that the money has not, as yet, been expended.
How many contracts have been awarded since the Armistice and what is the total amount involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Eighteen contracts
have been let since the Armistice was signed. If any hon. member wishes to refer to these contracts or any of the correspondence, I will be very glad to Table the documents. There is nothing that I wish to hide, or the Government either.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Might I ask the hon. member a question? Do I understand him to say that to-day in England, Ireland or Scotland ships of the same type as the Government has built can be bought at $105 per ton?
I understand that the British Government is selling ships at the present time at less than $100 a ton.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is not an answer to my question. Did I understand my hon. friend to say that ships of a type similar to those that are being built in our Canadian yards can be built in any yards of the United Kingdom at $105 a ton or at any lower price than what the Canadian Government is paying?

My hon. friend has got that competition before him; all the ships on the sea are competing for that one cargo. And my hon. friend has told the House over and over again that he is charging the market rate. Now, I want to know what benefit it is to the farmer of Canada if his wheat or his cattle is carried to the Liverpool market at exactly the same rate in a Gavernment ship as in a private ship? And what can be the benefit to the taxpayer if he has to pay the deficit that my hon. friend is bound to have to make good when he enters into competition with those ships that were built at a lower price? It is a very simple calculation. I have stated that a large number of ships with which my hon. friend is competing are ships that were built before the war at a price of from $50 to $60 a ton. Great Britain, at the time the war broke out, had some twenty million tons of shipping on the seas, and a large part of that tonnage was built at those low rates.
Very many of those ships are still on the seas, and my hon. friend when the times get hard-and they are getting harder now for shipping owners, ships are idle to-day in the harbours of New York and Boston because they cannot find business-will have to meet close competition. Let us make a comparison between the conditions pertaining to the building of a ship, say, at Halifax and those prevailing in connection with the building of a similar ship in the Old Country. My hon. friend, I understand, is having two ships built at Halifax at the rate of $195 a ton. At this rate, One 10,000 ton ship will cost him $1,950,000. The insurance on that ship cannot be less than three per cent of the value of the hull; the cost of insurance, therefore, when he starts the ship in business will be $58,500. He must allow five per cent for depreciation if he expects to continue in the business and get his capital back; that will be $97,500. He tells us that he is making five per cent interest on his money; that is another $97,500. The total amount of fixed charges, therefore, on the ship is $253,500. Now, let us take a ship built on the Clyde prior to the war at $60 a ton- a 10,000 ton ship of exactly the same type, with which my hon. friend has to compete. The cost of the ship in the first place would be $600,000. The insurance on the hull at three per cent would be $18,000; depreciation at five per cent, $30,000; interest at five per cent, $30,000; in all $78,000. These two ships are competing for the same business; one has a fixed charge of $253,500; the other a fixed charge of $78,000, to that the 
handicap against my hon. friend's ship to begin with is $175,000. That is to say, he has to earn with his ship $175,000 more than the other man earns before he can begin to pay a profit. When times are hard and freights are low, it will be impossible for him to do that, and the business must end up with a very heavy loss to me people of this country.
I drew the attention of the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) this evening to the fact that he had not given a bookkeeping statement with regard to this business of running the railways. I want to make the same remark to the Minister of Marine. He has not given a statement-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is here.

You can read his speech very carefully without finding any statement showing assets and liabilities. My hon. friend is a business man; he knows what I want. If he was giving the financial statement of a joint stock company in Montreal of which he was director or president, he would show all his assets and all his liabilities; he would show also his profit and loss account; and he would place it in such shape that a business man could take up that piece of paper and see whether the shareholders were making or losing money. He has not given us any such statement. He told the committee the other night that he had somewhere a million and a half dollars in cash and in Victory bonds. Well, I quite believe he has, but in the other pocket he may have bills amounting to a million and a half that are not paid. I do not know what his liabilities are; nobody knows; nobody can tell from the statement that he has given. If we are going into the business of running ships; if we are going into the business of running railways, we must be business men and treat the people of this country as the president of a company treats his shareholders,-that is, give them a fair statement showing just how we stand. Does any one in this country know whether or not my hon. friend is making money in this business? I am quite willing to take his word for it, but he would not need to make a speech to convince me if he gave a proper statement from which I could see for myself. I was unfortunately absent when he made his speech the other day, but I read it over very carefully and it looked to me as if he was making an apology for what he was doing. I have a suspicion that he himself has not very much faith in this scheme and that he already sees the end

of it. He does not say that he is going to continue it.
The Minister of Railways came to the rescue of my hon. friend the other night by saying that we must have ships in order to carry on the business of the country; we must have them in order to compete with the Canadian Pacific. The Canadian Pacific, he argued, has ships; therefore the Government of Canada, if it is to prosecute the business of running a railway, must also have ships to carry the traffic from Canadian ports and route it through to its destination. Now, that might be true if the Government were establishing a line of ships on the Atlantic to carry passengers and freight across to Liverpool or other ports. That would be business. But that is not what the Government are doing; they are sending their ships all over the world. And I challenge my hon. friend to show where he is going to get his return cargo. Suppose he sends a ship from St. John down to the river Plate with a load of lumber. When he gets there, there is no return cargo to bring to Canada. What will he do? Will he buy coal at an enormous rate at the river Plate, where it costs three or four times as much as it costs up here, and will he fill his ship with that coal and steam all the way back to St. John with nothing in the hold? He will not do it if he is a business man; so that if he Is going to continue the operation of his tramp vessel he must send it somewhere else. Well, the chances are that he will find a cargo of cattle or of wheat for Liverpool; nothing else will pay him. What will *he be doing then? He will be developing the trade of the Argentine and competing in the Liverpool market with the Canadian farmer. That is the kind of liner he is going to run; he cannot avoid it if he continues to do business as he is doing it now. He is not bulding liners; he is not establishing any line of ships. The Minister of Railways need not worry over making terms with outside steamships to carry his traffic across the Atlantic. Dozens of steamships which cross the Atlantic from Montreal, Halifax, St. John and various points in Canada will be glad to connect up with the Canadian National railways and carry their traffic to the other side on easy terms. My hon. friend would have no trouble in making a good bargain, because there are many of these ships and they would all be competing for the business. It is idle to say that you cannot carry on a railway business without having ships to carry your produce across the ocean. Very few railway companies in 57
the world have their own ships. England and Scotland send out as much produce as any other country in the world, but the railway companies of these countries do not, as a rule have their own ships. Very few of the United States railway companies have ships; it is very easy for them to make arrangements for the routing of their traffic through to destination. That argument, therefore, does not hold, though it was the chief argument advanced by the Minister of Railways the other night in defence of my hon. friend's policy.
I do not wish the Minister of Marine to think that I am opposed to Canadian shipbuilding, for I am not. No man is more anxious than I am to see the Canadian flag on the Seven Seas, and anything that can be done in that direction I shall support. But my hon. friend will never see that until he reduces his tariff. No protective country has ever been able to build up a great mercantile marine. For many years past no country would have been better able to do it than the United States. But it was a reproach to the United 'States, and they felt the reproach, that their passengers and their freight were carried in British ships across the ocean; that only some 12 per cent of their trade was carried in their own ships. It was a reproach to the people of the United States, and they would have overcome it if they could, but they could not overcome it and at the same time maintain their high tariff. Similarly, rwe cannot build up a mercantile marine and at the same time maintain our high tariff. If hon. members will look at the tariff schedules, they will find scores of articles that enter into the construction of ships that -are made more expensive by the tariff. The only other way of assisting the shipbuilding industry rwill be by a bounty, and personally, I am not in favour of a bounty; I think the only effective step is a reduction in the tariff if the minister expects the Canadian people to continue in the shipbuilding industry. We have a good example in the province from which I come. Many years ago, Nova Scotia was one of the greatest shipbuilding countries in the world, for its population. That is a big statement to make, but I make it advisedly. Fifty years ago, more or less, no other country in the world had as many tons of shipping on the sea as Nova Scotia had in proportion to its population; it had a ton of shipping for every inhabitant, for every man, woman and child in the province, and that figure has not, I believe, been reached by any other country. Great Britain has



a very large fleet of ships, as hon. members know; the minister told us that when war broke out she had over twenty million tons of shipping; but Great Britain at that time had a population of over 40,000,000 people, and she was the only country that could compete with Nova Scotia in tonnage. Nevertheless, in proportion to population, Nova Scotia had double the tonnage that Great Britain had. How did we get that large tonnage? We got it under what was practically a free trade policy. We had a 10 to 12 per cent tariff in Nova Scotia at that date. The ships were wooden ships. They were built from the wood of Nova Scotia; work was done by the people of Nova Scotia, the hulls were built of wood and also the fastenings, and when a hull was finished some merchant in Glasgow or Liverpool advanced the builder the rigging, sails and other material, and that was admitted into the province free. That was practically free trade, and that was the way in which Nova Scotia made such great progress in wooden shipbuilding. I quite understand hon. members will say that when iron replaced wood we could not carry on the industry; but I can assure my hon. friend that we did carry it on under a low tariff, and we carried it on successfully. I may also make the statement to him that no country in the history of the world that maintained a high tariff ever had a great mercantile fleet. Therefore, to my mind, there is just one solution and only one. I am distinctly opposed to Government ownership. It is not the part of this Government to play the game; the Government should referee the game and let the people play it. Let my hon. friend produce some kind of a policy by which the people of this country can embark in the shipbuilding industry and he will have my hearty support.

Before the minister concludes, I should like to. be permitted to say a few words on this vote. I think the House *and the country are indebted to the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) for having held the vote over. We are getting a little more daylight on this question than we did the last time it was debated in this House.
Louder. .

Does my hon. friend mean that? It may be his hearing and not my voice that is wrong., I am, however, very glad to accommodate him. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) has just delivered a speech of very

great political wisdom and importance, and I am personally gratified to have support from him for views which I modestly put before the House last week when this subject was under discussion. His voice on this question is a weighty voice, because noother hon. gentleman in this House knows about the shipping question better than the hon. .member for Guysborough. I can only hope his reward will be better than mine-was for having given sound views on political economy. When I tried to preach the same doctrines, my genial and eccentric .friend the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Butts) was put on his feet to ask me if I ever heard of Christopher Columbus. I am glad to see my hon. friend in his place and to relieve his anxiety about my historical knowledge; I have heard of the gentleman, but I have not quite the opinion that my hon. friend appears to have of him as a discoverer. I came to America much later than Christopher Columbus, and I found things here that Christopher Columbus never dreamed of-my hon. friend, for example.
I find nothing that reflects on myself in the first part of the speech of the hon. member for Guysborough. He uses stronger language than I care to use-I am well known to be a man of moderate views and studiously and carefully guarded language. Therefore, .when the minister came with his shipping projects before the House about twelve months ago, I expressed fear that he had entered into what was an unprofitable contract. The hon. member for Guysborough changes the words slightly, and he boldly charges my hon. friend with a profiteering contract. II judge my meaning was the same, but I always like to be careful in the use of language. With regard to that, I must repeat that I think these contracts have not been profitable. I must say, when I raised this question first, I did not get the support'll expected from the official Opposition of the day. The occasion was a somewhat famous one, and my hon. friend, the then leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) made it the occasion of a declaration, which I believe was a very serious declaration for himself. On that occasion he stated, with that honesty and courage which are characteristic of him, that he was a protectionist, and I am afraid that that declaration cost him the leadership of the party. I always hate to see any hon. gentleman suffer for his honesty. Sitting where he does, it is all right for one to entertain protectionist

views, but it is very wrong to avow them. But my advice will be of no use to my hon. friend now. 1 say that I did not get the support 1 expected on that occasion from the official Opposition. I am all the more glad to see my old and honoured friend, the member for Guysborough, strike out from the shoulder in the way he did to-night. I am deeply grateful to him for enforcing my views on political economy as I expressed them last week.
II did not rise to delay this vote, but I understand that we have the assurance of the minister that this is to carry out contracts which have already been entered into, and that after that he and the Government are retiring from the shipbuilding business. I understand that is the position at which we have arrived on this question. If I am not right, no doubt the minister will put me right when he rises to reply presently.
While I am on my feet, I wish to make reference to another matter which arose in this debate last week, and I do so for the purpose of making the position of this party in this House and in the country very clear upon	a subject which,	I understood	from the minister, the Government have under their consideration, and that is the subject of possible subsidies to ships. I understand that the minister will finish these contracts and go out of what, according to. my hon. friend from Guysborough, has been a profiteering business. I do not know that we should be surprised that it is such a business. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine comes from Montreal, and his deputy comes from Nova Scotia. Well, coming from the West as 1 do, I, a priori, have arrived at the conclusion that this is not a very good combination with regard to shipbuilding for the rest of Canada,-my hon. friend from Guysborough is an exception, of course, to certain -tendencies in Nova Scotia, he still retains the free trade instincts of his family, but I am afraid there are very strong protectionists among the Liberals of Nova Scotia besides my hon. friend the late leader of the Opposition.. However, the profiteering business is to be stopped, and the Government are considering the question pi subsidies. Now I do not know whether my hon. friend from South Cape Breton was speaking in favour of subsidies or not; I am not at all sure that he knew himself. He said some things, nevertheless. He is always interesting to listen to, and thoroughly good-natured as a rule. I do not know that he was so very good-natured when he dis-57i
avowed his Irishism and proclaimed himsell a Canadian. I presume he meant by birth. I think I knew the meaning of his strong expression as well as of the enthusiastic cheers which accompanied that avowal of his nationality. All I have got to say upon that is this, that in opposing subsidies to British companies if they are going to make profiteering contracts or plunder the taxpayers of -Canada I am a better Canadian and am less of an Englishman than my hon. friend if he supports the subsidies. It is only a poor type of Canadian in this House who does not feel it his duty to look after the cash of the people whom he is sent here to represent, rather than to allow those people to be rooked by companies, let those companies be from England or wherever you like.
I did not last week get the unanimous support I should have liked from the Opposition on the question of subsidies. Indeed, the two official sides have a very strong resemblance to one another on all these questions. There are hon. members opposite who come from the farming districts of Ontario who have very little use for' subsidies, just'as there are in the official Opposition hon. -gentlemen who come from agricultural areas, who have very little use for subsidies. On the otherhand,justasmy hon. friend from Toronto spoke strongly in favour of subsidies, so my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) seemed rather in a receptive mood, and he said, that if such things were going round and there was money to provide them, he would be there with his hand out-so I understood him. I Ho not know that my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) if he were present, would deny that he himself would look for a subsidy for shipping if such things were going. The hon. member for Cape Breton too I think would have an appetite in that direction. So we -see, Mr. Chairman, that in regard to the two official sides of this House there is not very much difference between the two parties, any .more than there was a year ago, in regard to this profiteering contract, between the then leader of the Opposition and the Minister of Marine.
But I want to say that there is a party in this House, which is much larger in the country, and behind which there is a swelling tide, which is absolutely at one both-on profiteering contracts and on subsidies. We here, to a man, are opposed to subsidies and .bounties on principle. We say they are unjust, they are bad political economy, they are wrong, and we oppose them, we care not what riding wants them. We are looking after the interests, the broad;

interests of the whole Canadian people. When you pay a bounty to Dominion Steel,
* or a subsidy to shipbuilders, to placate the electors of a certain constituency, where do ; you get the money? Some one addressed [DOT] that question to the minister the other day, sand in the innocence of his heart he said. "I think we will get it from the bank." When you get money from a bank, the bank is not acting like the Good Samaritan-the money has to be paid back. Where does the money come from for all these doles? It comes from the brawn and sinew of the labourer, from the twelve hours' day of the farmer, from the worker in the factories. It comes out of the blood and bone and muscle of the people. We say it is a wrong thing to spend in bounties and subsidies money that has been got in that way. So we are opposed to subsidies on principle, and we are so opposed to a man.
I want to make one more point in this connection before I sit down. We are especially opposed to subsidies at this time because of the financial conditions of the country. I am trying to give the Government some grounds on which to come to a wise decision on policy, which we have been told by the minister is to be communicated to us when the financial statement for the year is brought down. The Government lias no money to throw away in subsidies at the present time. The Government are living on borrowed money. They have just taken $700,000,000 from the people of this country, and the Lord only knows in His dwelling place when they will be able to pay it back unless we change our fiscal policy. They have neither moral right nor ' financial status to give subsidies of this hind. What the people of this country -want is honest housekeeping. They want their money taken care of, and it is only by taking care of it and by arranging taxation on a proper basis that we shall alter the exchange against us in the United States, reduce the cost of living, and make Canada a fit country for heroes to dwell in.
. I have one more ground supplied to me by my kind and genial friend from South Cape Breton. He told us in his address last week that they got the cheapest ore 'from Newfoundland that is to be found on the face of the earth. I do not think I misrepresent my hon. friend-the cheapest iron ore in the world.
, Mr. BUTTS: What I did say was that we were capable of producing on the shores of Sydney harbour the cheapest pig iron in the world.

From the splendid
ores of Newfoundland they are capable of producing on the shores of Sydney harbour the cheapest pig iron in the world. Capable? Then capable men do not want subsidies. That is the argument. If you have the cheapest ore, and you are capable men, then take the advice of my hon. friend from Guysborough: Go to it and build ships in competition with the world.
i Mr. BUTTS: I might tell my hon. friend from Red Deer, as he comes from a farming country, that we do not build ships out of pig iron.

I might tell my hon.
friend, though I come from a farming country, that he cannot build them without .pig iron. Does my hon. friend wish another exchange? Mr. Chairman, I am a Canadian, and I wish to induce Canadian-ism, but not of the puny kind that comes to this House seeking subsidies. I want to produce Canadians who can stand four square to all the winds that blow, as their forefathers did in the Islands of the North sea, and as their brothers did in the trenches in Flanders. I -want Canadians who in the trade and manufacturing world can stand four square to all the winds that blow, and say to competition, let it come from where it will: We are capable men; we have the material and we can produce the goods. That is the kind of Canadian-ism I believe in.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am greatly surprised that the member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) should charge this Government in face of the information I have placed before the House, with having placed profiteering contracts. I take issue squarely with both hon. gentlemen and aver emphatically that not one profiteering contract has been placed. It is all very fine for hon. members, possibly for political reasons, to level such a serious charge against me as a responsible minister, and against the Government. But before this House and the public of Canada will accept the allegation that profiteering contracts have been placed by this Government, these hon. gentlemen must adduce more substantial proof than merely making the charge , and letting it go at that. The hon. member for Guysborough did me the hpnour to confess that he had carefully read every word of my speech, and then alleged that profiteering contracts had been placed, stating that ships could be built in the United Kingdom at lower prices than those at which the Can-

adian Government had placed their contracts. I am sorry to take up the time of the House, but in view of the first charge of dishonesty that has ever been levelled at this Government or any member of the Government, I wish to quote again the figures I quoted the other day.

I rise to a point of order. Nothing I stated could be construed into a charge of dishonesty against the minister. When I talked of unprofitable contracts I meant the profits which the Government should have saved for the country went to those who sold steel plates at a dearer rate than that at which they should have been sold. That is not a charge of dishonesty against the minister. I had no such thought in my mind, and no word of my language will bear that interpretation.
It is bad business.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am glad to hear
the statement of the hon. member for Red Deer. I certainly understood him to say that profiteering contracts had been placed for ships, but if I am wrong I accept with very good grace the hon. gentleman's assurance that he did not intend to convey the impression that profiteering contracts had been placed by this Government.

My hon. friend
must not misunderstand me. I endorse the position taken by the hon. member for Guysborough, but a distinction must be made between profiteering by contractors with whom the minister does business, and profiteering by the minister himself, which would be the only thing that could justify a charge of dishonesty.

During the war?
Mr. BALLANTYNE':	During the war.
Most of our contracts had been placed during the war, and since the Armistice was signed the Canadian Government ordered ships at $167.50 per ton; and I say from my place in this House that for a similar type of ship placed at the same time no one could have obtained in England, Ireland or Scotland a lower rate than $167.50.

Has the minister any
figures to substantiate that statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Certainly. The
figures I quoted just now are the official figures of the Committee on National Expenditure of the British Government. That is my authority.

Were these contracts
placed during the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I presume the orders for these ships were placed during the war.

If the hon. gentleman will permit me. Earlier in the evening he mentioned that contracts for eighteen of these ships had been awarded since the signing of the armistice. Has the hon. gentleman any figures to show the price per ton of other ships, the contracts for which were given about the same time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: No, no.
What was the rate of exchange?
At what date?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: May of last year.

Can the hon. gentleman tell the committee the price per ton in the case of any contract for ships placed by well known private corporations, for instance such as the Canadian Pacific Railway, about the same time as he placed these orders for ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will not give the name of the firm that ordered the ships because I do not think I would be right in doing so. I can say this, however, that Norway has placed orders for ships with one of our yards in this country within the last three months, at $170 per ton, and France has also placed an order at $170 per ton. I can say further that the Canadian Government have been offered not only the price that we are paying for our ships but more if we choose to sell them.
Then the hon. gentleman has no figures with respect to orders given by Canadian firms upon which to base a comparison?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, 1 do not know anything about the orders given by any Canadian firm, but the very fact of Norway and France placing orders in Canada within the last three months at prices higher than the Canadian Government are paying, is, I think, conclusive evidence that ours are not profiteering contracts.
Is the $167 per ton the lowest price, or the average price, of the 18 ships referred to?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The lowest price.
What was the highest price?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: For what period?
I would like to know the highest price at which contracts were let for any of the 18 ships since the signing of the armistice.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Shortly after the signing of the armistice a contract was placed at $170 per ton and that is the highest price that has been paid for that type of ship-that is the largest type, of 8,400 tons deadweight. Most of these orders were placed at $167.50 per ton. I also stated last week that the firm of Skinner and Eddie, of Seattle, are constructing standard vessels of 8,800 tons. Mr. Skinner, when giving testimony before the United States Senate last month, declared that these vessels were being constructed at the present time at a price of $185 per ton. Now, I think, Sir, that I have proved my case, that no profiteering contracts have been let. I have also proved that the United States, their programme being much larger than ours, have paid $25 per ton and upwards more than we have paid. I have shown the price that the Imperial Munitions Board have paid for steel ships, and for wooden ships, and I have shown the price that Great Britain has paid for steel ships during the war. I have stared what the price is to-day for similar ships built in the United Kingdom and built here. 1 have given all these figures, which are absolutely accurate and official, and neither the Canadian Government nor this Parliament should be ashamed of the prices at which we have placed our contracts. Ie: me repeat again, there is no justification for the charge that has been made as to placing profiteering contracts.
The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. [DOT]Sinclair) stated that he has some doubts as to the net profit of $1,406,000 that I stated a week ago resulted from the operation of the 19 ships that were in commission last year, some of which had only made one trip. The hon. gentleman states that as a business man, before making such a statement to the House, I should be prepared to lay before it the usual business statement showing assets and liabilities. I am glad to tell the hon. gentleman that I have

If the hon. member for Guys-borough doubts' that statement, I would like, with the unanimous consent of the committee, to place on Hansard a statement of the gross and net profit of each one of these ships for each voyage.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
These profits, as I
have already stated, were .arrived at in the .same way that any business house would arrive at profits. After providing for organization, overhead expenses, depreciation, interest on the ships and insurance, the net profit has been arrived at, the amount being as stated.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) takes a more gloomy and pessimistic view of the Government ownership of ships than I do. I am a thorough believer in the Government ownership and operation of ships. Where would Canada have been during the past year if it had not been for the Government ships that brought a vast amount of tonnage of raw sugar from the West Indies to the sugar refineries of Canada at Halifax, St. John and Montreal? There would have been an actual sugar shortage in this country. Where would the people of British Columbia have been with respect to the large amount of lumber that they had in that province if it had not been for the Government ships which carried that lumber to England, to Australia and to New Zealand?
It has been stated by the hon. gentleman that ships operated by private ownership are going empty either one way or the other. I am happy to tell the hon. gentleman that the Government ships have full cargoes both going and coming on the various routes on which they are operating. I do not wish to unnecessarily occupy the time of the House, but let me cite the case of the Canadian Pioneer that runs to Buenos Ayres. The gross earnings of that vessel on the outward voyage were
$174,961.17. On the return voyage the gross earnings were $292,000.
What cargo did she bring back?	'

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Hides and other goods. I cannot give you the precise details of the composition of her cargo.
Did she bring that cargo to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Some of it here and some of it to New York. But that does not make any difference. What I am trying to refute is the statement of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) to the effect that these vessels did not have return cargoes.
He did not say that. He said they did not bring return cargoes to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Most of these ships did bring return cargoes to Canada, but part of this particular ship's cargo was destined for the port of New York.
What did she bring to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. member will wait until I get through I will be glad to give him any information he wants. The total gross earnings of the " Canadian Pioneer " for that one voyage from Montreal to Buenos Aires were $466,961.17, and the net earnings were $214,828.27. As I stated, I have in my hand the gross earnings and the net earnings for the open voyages and for the closed voyages, and I will be very glad to hand it to the hon. member for Guysborough, or if the House prefers I will place the statement on the pages of Hansard.
Has the minister got a statement there of the steamer " McKee "?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is not a ship that was built under the Government's shipbuilding programme, she was bought several years ago and operated by the Railway Department. I have none of these old ships in my statement, only the new ships that have been built and operated under the Government's shipbuilding programme.
Was she not bought with money voted by this Government for the purchase of ships two or three years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I can only say that such purchase has not been out of any

votes that have been put through the House for the Government shipbuilding programme since I have had the honour of being Minister of Marine. Before I resume my seat I want to say that with our large transcontinental railway system of 22,000 miles this House would be ill-advised, in my humble opinion, if it did not endorse the Government ownership and operation of these ships in order to compete with the Canadian Pacific railway. Not only do these ships make the profit that I have stated, but co-operating with them our railway system makes a profit also on the long fiaul.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will put it in another way that probably will better please hon. members opposite. I want to say that the .deficits on railway operation would have been even greater than what the hon. Minister of Railways has stated to-day did w'e not have these ships working in cooperation with our railway system.
Absolutely not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Well, I differ from my hon. friend there. 1 am quite willing to adopt the policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway. There is no better managed corporation than the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and if the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have seen fit to operate a large fleet of cargo and passenger ships in conjunction with their railway system, and to keep their marine accounts separate from their railway accounts in order to be able to tell what profit each branch is making, the Government of Canada cannot be wrong in following that policy. It has come to my notice since I have been minister, and I knew it before, that all transatlantic steamers are controlled by pooled rates. As a result Canada has been discriminated against time and again. How can we expand our export trade to South Africa, the West Indies and to other countries unless we own our own ships? Even if Canada did not make a cent on her ships, -I will go further than that and say, even if she made a loss,-the Government would be fully justified in carrying out their programme of owning and operating these ships. From what I have seen of the advantages of these ships in extending Canada's export trade, and also of the benefit accruing to our railway system from their operation, I am convinced that when the days of keener competition come, if those engaged in farming, mining, lumbering and manufacturing,
[Mr. Ballantyne.l
either directly or as middlemen, find they cannot compete with other countries on account of our freight rates being a little high, I for one would think the Canadian Government Merchant Marine would be fully justified in lowering those rates in order that the products of our farms, mines, forests and factories could be delivered in any foreign countries on a basis that would [DOT]enable our exporters to compete with the rest of the world. Therefore I will say as I take my seat that not only do I believe enthusiastically in the Government shipbuilding programme, but, without wishing to assume the role of a prophet, I also believe that if we are spared to meet here a year hence we shall be able to show a very much larger profit statement than the one I have already submitted to the House.

I differ from my hon. friend in his statement that we cannot build up an export trade without owning a merchant marine. He has made that statement constantly, and, in my judgment, it is without foundation. It is low freight rates that give a country a chance to build up an export trade, and you do not get low freight rates under government manage-merit. At the time the ships came under government management in Great Britain, the freight rates went up something like 58 per cent, and in some cases as high as 85 per cent, and when the same ships went back into private ownership the freight rates dropped again. That is what happened in England. Low rates will give you a chance to export; high rates will cripple you. Surely the Government of Great Britain is just as anxious to build up export trade as is the Government of Canada at the present moment, yet what is the Government of Great Britain doing? It is selling every ton of shipping it owns and putting the ships back into private hands, and it is selling them at a price a little more than one-half of what my hon. friend is paying now for the ships he is building to compete with those very ships for the export' trade. The Government of the United States is just as anxious to build up an export trade as my hon. friend can be, but what is that Government doing? It is making arrangements to transfer all the ships it holds into private hands, and the price is mentioned at about $100 a ton. When my hon. friend says that export trade cannot be built up by a country without the Government owning the merchant marine, I want to tell him that it has been done. No country in the world has built up such an export trade as Great Britain, it has beaten

the world in exports, and imports as well, and while doing that it did not own one ton of shipping. My hon. friend will have to revise his information on that question before he is very much older.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to confirm in two words what my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) has said about Great Britain. I daresay many hon. members read'the very informing article in last nights' papers from an American correspondent in London pointing out that Great Britain since it parted with its government ships and sent them hack to private ownership has exported more goods in the month of February just past than it had exported in any given month since the beginning of the war, that is, since the year 1914, and that those exports were going up every day. That is the condition of affairs under private ownership in Great Britain, which country, after all, does know something about shipping and cuts quite a figure in the shipping world.
But my main purpose in rising was to deal with a much more important statement of my hon. friend. A week ago he stated that the money we are voting now was to end existing contracts, and that on their completion the Government was going out of the business.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is right.
Then I need say no more. I hope my hon. friend does not misunderstand me.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. member will allow me, I made the statement before, and I make.it now, that the Government has finished its shipbuilding programme. I presume that is what my hon. friend refers to.

I am very glad to hear that assurance; it simplifies the proceeding of getting this vote through so far as I am concerned. But in his speech to-night I certainly understood my hon. friend to express a very enthusiastic opinion in the direction of the Government's continuing this business, and I thought that statement not consistent with the interpretation, which it appears was correct, which I had put upon his statement when this matter Was previously before us.

I understood the minister
to say last week that as the result of the operation of these nineteen steamers he had #1,500,000 cash in bank and Victory bonds. He told us also that there was a net profit
of $1,400,000. To-night he tells us that he has only #432,000 in the bank and $504,000 ,in Victory bonds, a total of $936,000. There is a discrepancy which I should like the minister to explain.
[ Mr. BALLANTYNE: Accounts receivable are also considered as cash; these amount to $492,247.75. Outstanding freight is also included.
i Mr. DUFF: I admit that I am not much nf a business man, but I never heard tell of accounts receivable being put in the bank as cash. If that is the way the Minister of Marine does business, the quicker he sells his ships the better. Accounts receivable are not cash, therefore the Minister of Marine deliberately misled this committee when he told us that he had $1,,500,000 by way of cash in the bank and Victory bonds.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member to withdraw the words " deliberately misled."

Well, unintentionally misled the committee. There is no question that there is not $1,500,000 in the bank. The minister also told us that there were liabilities of $627,000 and outstanding accounts payable amounting to $340,000, a total of $967,000. According to these figures, instead of having $1,400,000 to his credit, the minister has only $500,000. Then, he does not allow for depreciation. If he can offer an explanation of that I shall be glad to hear it.
, Mr. BALLANTYNE: I have said on more than one occasion that the net profits were arrived at after providing for operating expenses, overhead, depreciation, interest on cost of ships, and insurance. If the hon. member wishes me to read the figures again I will do so, but they are as I gave them a moment ago.

I would like to have the
thing explained so that the committee will understand it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Very well. The current assets of the company are as follows: Cash in banks, $432,576.13; Victory bonds, which are the same as cash, $504,583.33; accounts receivable-I said, not that they were cash, but that they were equal to cash-1492,247.75; outstanding freight, $71,411.05; material and supplies, $1,668.87; a total of $1,502,487.13. Equipment, $8,502.03. Deferred charges:	insurance, $505,284.27;
advance wages, etc., $8,263.97; grand total of assets, $2,024,537.40.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I assume that it
would mean office furniture, and so on.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has the minister a list of the contracts that have been awarded since November 11, 1918, and their amounts?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My deputy will get the information and I will give it to iny hon. friend when it is ready.
Did the United States have a government-owned mercantile marine?

I am not discussing the
subsidies to vessels; I am referring to the suggestion which is frequently made that Great Britain has passed all other countries in the matter of foreign trade and pointing out that according to these figures, which are absolutely reliable, the United States and Germany have surpassed Great Britain in percentage of increase of foreign trade.

Without any government
mercantile marine?

Referring for a moment to the interesting figures placed before the House by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), 1 wish first to say that he is using the very unsound percentage comparisons . which were the fundamental unsoundness of the abortive campaign for protection which Mr. Joseph Chamberlain carried on in England some fifteen or eighteen years ago. Of course, the percentage of progress made by people who come into a race later than their competitors who have been in the race fol years, is bound to be much greater than the percentage of progress made by the latter. For instance, let us imagine that Nova Scotia had a fleet of 1,000 vessels and that Prince Edward Island had a fleet of four vessels, and that in one year the fleet of Nova Scotia increased to 1,500 vessels, which would be an increase of 50 per cent, while the Prince Edward Island fleet increased to eight vessels, or an increase of 100 per cent. According to the arguments of my hon. friend across the way, the progress of Prince Edward Island would have been twice as great as that of Nova Scotia. That is precisely the basis of his interesting figures placed before the committee.
To return to the subject matter of the debate of to-night, I am going to make a last appeal to the minister to get out of this business when he can do so with a profit. The minister is in a peculiar position tonight. He has told us, with one breath: I believe in government ownership and operation of vessels, and again in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) he has, if I mistake not, said that after these ships are built, the Government is at the end of its shipbuilding programme, and-I presume he will correct me if I am wrong-its ship-operating programme.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. member will allpw me, I did not make any statement about the operation of the ships other than that they were operated and managed by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. The reason the Government have ceased placing contracts for freight ships is because we consider that with 63 steamships with a net tonnage of 380,000 tons, we have ample tonnage to take care of whatever export trade the ships might be called upon to carry or whatever other service they might be called upon to perform in conjunction with the government railways.

First, as to the statement that it is the Canadian Merchant Marine Limited that carries on the business, that is merely a naval uniform for the Government. The "Government will be and will remain, in the eyes of the people responsible, and I should like to know- the minister, I am sure, will tell me- whether it is the intention of the Government, once they have finished their shipbuilding programme, to go on with a ship-operating programme under the guise of this company.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

That places the matter before us fairly and squarely. I think the Government, in this policy, is making a grave error which, in the long run, will cost the taxpayers of this country large sums of money. The first reason for my belief is this:	The ships have been built at very
high prices. Before I touch on the question of price, I wish to revert for a moment to this situation, that 18 contracts which were let for the building of 18 ships, were let illegally and improperly. I want that fact to sink into the consciousness of the Canadian people. What has the minister said in defence of this irregularity? He has said:	I was very careful in letting
those contracts, and I saw to it that the price was a fair one; I drove a hard bargain with people on the other side. With all respect, I wish to tell the minister that that is no answer. It is not for the Minister of Marine, nor for anyone in charge of a Government department to say: I am above the law; the law, it is true, lays down certain rules for my guidance; but I thought that I could, for the benefit of the country, depart from those rules so laid down. That was improper conduct on the part of the minister, and I trust the people of Canada will take note of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Will the hon. member allow me a question? I think the hon. member heard his leader read the law?

Not only did I heal
my leader read the law, but I read the law myself to the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If my hon. friend
will allow me, 'when the armistice was signed, a great emergency existed in this country-

We are getting at cross purposes. I am not complaining as to the building of these ships before the armistice; I am complaining about the building ol ships after the armistice. In my opinion, no such pressing emergency existed once the armistice was signed as warranted the minister in departing from the law.
The next point I wish to make is this. The minister has said: I know that I did not let the contracts at too high a price, because during the war contracts were let at a very much higher price. That is not an answer. The minister might have said: Since the armistice has been signed, Great Britain, in her shipyards, has built on government account ships at so much per ton; the United States since the armistice has been signed, has built in her shipyards on Government account ships at so much per ton. The minister has not done that; he has, in order to justify his action, compared post-war prices which he granted after the armistice with prices which were granted while the war was on, and that is not a fail comparison. The point which I wish to make is how unsafe and unsound it. is for any. minister to depart from what I regard as the plain letter of the law.
What is the present situation? We are asked to vote money to build ships at about $195 per ton, when ships with which these ships have to compete are being built or at least are being sold-and it makes very little difference whether they are being built or sold in Great Britain and in the Untied States at roughly half that price. In an article taken from an English paper I read the other day that there are as many ships in the world to-day as there were at the outbreak of the war. Now, if that statement is correct, and I believe it is, the minister will very shortly have to compete with ships as numerous as those before the war, and a great number of these ships will be pre-war ships which were built at $55 or $60 a ton. The reason why high rates are still being earned is that many of the harbours of the world are overcrowded, and ships have therefore to wait for cargoes, and we have not the free circulation which we otherwise would have. But freights are dropping every day, the practical mariner from Lunenburg (Mr. COMMONS
Duff) assures me. I am glad the minister has made money for the Canadian, people so far, if he has made it-other experts say he has not-but, anyway, so far he has got along without a severe loss, and I am glad of it because the Canadian people need every red cent we can lay our hands on. But the point I want to make is this-I have made it before, and I do not wish to labour it-the operation of tramp steamers is not a proper function for a Government department. All we do require is the initiative and the liberty which private ownership will give.
The minister has called to his aid the Canadian Pacific. He tells us that the Canadian Pacific own ships on the sea. Yes, they own the big transatlantic and transpacific liners for the purpose of rounding out their transcontinental system. But that is not the sort of boats the minister is building or proposes to build. If he was proposing to build 14,000-ton or 15,000-ton liners there would be something in that argument, but as he is building only tramp steamers of 8,000, 6,000, 4,000 and down to 2,200 deadweight tonnage, his argument falls to the ground. We have had an example both in the United States and Great Britain of government ownership of steamers. These two great nations have seen fit to return to private ownership. Is their example worth nothing to the minister? I venture to assert that there is hardly a shipping man in Montreal who agrees with the proposal of the minister and with the policy he has adopted. .

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Hear, hear. Not
one.
Mr. MeMASTER: I suppose the minister will say that is merely selfishness on their part. The minister has already said his line is subsidized, that if it does not pay for itself the deficit will be made up out of taxes. I wish to take emphatic issue with the minister there. A public service, whether it is publicly or privately owned, should pay for itself and stand on its own feet. The proposal that you should take certain activities of the Canadian people and socialize them, and then ask the whole Canadian people to make up the loss in operation is, I think, unjust. I believe it will not work. I believe experience has taught us that it has not worked in the past, and I believe it will not work in the future. We are dealing with vast sums of money in this matter. I presume that the minister will be able to get his vote through, in view of the large majority of members

of this House who sit behind him, but I wish to raise my voice in protest against a grave mistake and a deep wrong to the Canadian people, and I only hope and wish the minister will heed my words.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member
for Brome (Mr. McMaster) has pleaded eloquently and well for the agents of private steamship companies in the city of Montreal, from which city we both come, but that does not alter my opinion nor the opinion of the Government. Although my hon. friend heard the law quoted by his leader, he still says that contracts for 18 ships were illegally let. I repeat again, a great emergency existed. After the signing of the armistice we were bringing back hundreds of thousands of our returned soldiers.
Mr. MeMASTER: How many returned soldiers were brought back in Government ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None, but that does not alter my argument. The leader of the Opposition has cited the law, and within the confines of that law the Government ordered these eighteen ships. There was an emergency at that time. The whole country was upset. Thousands and thousands of men were out of work after the signing of the armistice. Hundreds of thousands of our brave men were returning from the front, and aside from the need for ships, which I claim the Government needed badly, a responsibility rested on the Government of providing work for the thousands of men who were out of work in this country at that time and for the large number of soldiers who were returning from day to day.
How long would it have taken to call for tenders in the ordinary way, assuming there was an emergency?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have already gone over that ground several times, and I do not think it is necessary for me to go over it again. However, I do not want to be discourteous, and I will explain in a few words. With seventeen yards calling for public tenders and six out of the seventeen quoting lower than the balance of the yards, how could we have kept the whole seventeen yards employed to relieve the unemployment situation?- I say that the Government kept within the law in placing these eighteen contracts since the armistice was signed.
Was there an emergency in January and February of this year, when I believe some contracts were let?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, I will come to that later. The hon. member for Brome apparently did not hear what I stated. He says that I only quoted pre-war prices.

I do not want the minister to take me up wrongly. I said that the minister compared the prices of vessels ordered since the armistice with the prices of vessels built during the war, not before the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I still state that
the hon. member for Brome could not have listened to what I stated. Let me compare the prices paid by the Canadian Government for ships since the armistice with the prices paid by other countries. I have already given this information, but I have no objection to repeating it. A well-known steamship company in .the old land that has a line of steamers running to Montreal paid, when the rate of exchange was at $4.80, the price of $216 per ton as compared with Canada's price of $167.50. France paid $170 per ton since the signing of the armistice, Norway paid $170 per. ton, and the United States paid $185 per ton.
Will the minister inform us in what way the idle situation constituted an emergency that could justify the placing of the contracts without tenders being called for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am sure that the hon. member (Mr. Duff), who lives by the sea where there are not so many unemployed men as there are in other parts of the country, must be aware that the idle situation was one of the most serious problems with which the Government had to deal after the signing of the armistice. It was a matter of providing help for unemployed men, particularly returned soldiers, and under the law cited by the leader of the Opposition, a real emergency existed when such a large number of men were out of employment, apart altogether from the pressing need of getting the ships.

Is it not a fact that the
Government voted for out-of-work soldiers a sum of $40,000,000 of which only $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 was expended. I can hardly see where there could have been such an emergency, if among the class which might have been expected to be unemployed, we did not find it necessary to spend more than one-tenth of the amount voted for the purpose of meeting unemployment.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman argue that there were not thousands
and thousands of men out of work in all the large cities and towns throughout Canada after the signing of the armistice?

I am speaking of the
months of January and February this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Well, does my hon. friend say that in January and February of this year there were not thousands of men out of work in all the large centres?
No, no.

Apparently, from the Government returns there were not. If I remember rightly, during the month of January there were very few men out of work, at least if we accept the Government returns as given by the press. In any event, there was not sufficient unemployment to constitute such an emergency as would make it imperative that contracts should be given without tenders being called for.
Can the minister give us a statement as to the number of returned men employed in these shipyards?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I cannot give the
hon. member the exact figures. There were twenty-five thousand men employed in the shipyards in Canada, and an equal number were employed in the allied trades, such as the manufacture of marine engines, boilers, winches, chains, etc. I do not know, of course, exactly what * percentage were returned soldiers, but I think I can safely say that the returned soldiers comprised a very large percentage.
Is the information available?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The only way in
which we could obtain that information would be by writing to each of the shipyards.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister promised to give us a list of contracts.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. There were
forty-five contracts placed before the signing of the armistice, and the contracts that have been let since then are as follows: Canadian Vickers, 4; Tidewater Shipbuilders Ltd., 2; Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co., 5; Harbour Marine, Victoria, 2; Kingston, 2; Coughlan and Son, 6; Halifax Shipbuilders, 2; Nova Scotia Steel Co., 3; Prince Rupert Co., 2; British American Co., 2; Col-lingwood Shipbuilding Co., 3; Midland Shipbuilding Co., 1; Wallace Shipyards, 2; Dominion Shipbuilding Co., 2.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
These contracts were for the construction of ships. DO

they include the entire equipment and furnishings of the ships as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The whole thing is awarded in one contract; there is no separate contract for furnishings?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. The Government lets the contract at so much per ton, and its designs and specifications have to be followed. The shipbuilding company who get the contract have to place orders for the engines, boilers, and all the equipment that goes into the ship.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is there any specification requiring the boilers, etc., to be purchased in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are copies of the contracts available?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Certainly.
I understand that a ship called The Recruit was lost in the St. Lawrence. Has the minister received the insurance on that ship?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Canadian Government Merchant Marine, who operate the ships, insured this vessel, the cargo of which was also insured. She is lying at the mouth of the Saguenay river, and will be salvaged without difficulty. For the information of the hon. member I may say that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine places the insurance on vessels and looks after all matters of that nature.
She is abandoned to the underwriters?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
The Government is not interested in the cargo?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Has no money been received yet on account of the insurance? In the statement which the minister has given us has he taken this wreck into account? Is it a loss, or how does it stand in the statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Canadian Recruit, which was wrecked by heavy ice, does not enter into the statement I have presented to the House. I inquired of Mr. Hanna Whether the ship and cargo were fully insured* and he informed me that they were. The ship has been abandoned, to the underwriters, but whether or not they have paid any money to the Canadian

Government Merchant Marine, I cannot say.

What interest has the Government or Mr. Hanna in the cargo of the . ship? I may be wrong, but I understood, the minister to say that the cargo was insured by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. What interest can the Government have in the cargo?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The shippers insure the cargo.

A few days ago I made certain inquiries regarding a ship called the A. J. McKee, and the minister informed the House that at 31st December last there a balance against that ship of $269,254. Has that been charged against the profits of the operation of the ships during the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The statement I have given to the House does not include the steamship A. J. McKee, which was an old ship purchased by the Department, of Railways and Canals before this Government was elected; and the answer to which the hon. member now refers was not given by me but by the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid).

That ship, while it was purchased prior to the election, was acquired for the purpose of carrying freight, and was a part of the Government's policy. The fact that the ship was purchased in April, 1917, which I understand is the date, cannot affect the result. The minister, I think, should have charged that loss against the account, and should have given us a full and fair statement as to how the account stands. It occurs to me that it is not fair for the minister to give a statement leaving out the ship which made a large loss and putting in the vessel which made a profit.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Before the item carries I want to get some information from the minister which may be of interest to the shippers of this country. I met only to-day the representative of the largest firm of cattle shippers in Canada who told me that during the winter they were compelled to ship cattle via New York because there were no ships calling at Canadian ports that were equipped to properly store cattle for shipment across the Atlantic. I want to know from the minister if he proposes to so equip the Canadian Government vessels that they can take care of the Canadian livestock trade. Another matter upon which I want to get some information is this: He
I

made the statement that heretofore Canada hW been discriminated against in the matter of ocean transportation. It has been a complaint of the manufacturing interests of Canada that ocean freights discriminate in favour of the raw material and against the manufactured product; that is, that raw material oftentimes is carried at a cheaper rate than the equivalent of that material when manufactured. I would like to know from the minister what will be the policy of the Government in future in the matter of rates as between the manufactured product and the raw material. For instance, will wheat be carried cheaper than its equivalent number of bushels if put into flour? I think it would be only fair for the minister to make a statement on these matters at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In answer to the hon. member I beg to say that the gentleman to whom he refers in speaking of shipments of cattle called upon me to-day. I told him that I knew of no reason why the Canadian ships should not be fitted up so as to carry cattle, and no later than this morning I referred this gentleman's letter to the manager of the Canadian Government Mercantile Marine at Montreal. I hope that the manager will take steps to see that the ships are so fitted as to enable them to carry Canadian cattle. The other questions to which the hon. member referred-	*

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Before the minister gets away from that point, is the statement correct that Canadian cattle had to be shipped all the winter from New York because of the lack of shipping facilities from Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am sorry that I cannot definitely answer that question until I hear from the management of the Canadian Government Mercantile Marine. The other question the hon. member has put to me is rather a difficult one. I know of course the broad policy of the management of the Canadian Government Mercantile Marine. There is so much freight offering now that they are charging the same rates as any other company for similar freight. What they may do, however, when competition becomes keener, I do not know. Still, I can say this: That while not interfering with the company in any way at all, I suggested that when they found they could help Canadian shippers, no matter what the product shipped might be, by quoting a lower rate, I thought they would be justified in doing so.

I see around me a great number of hon. members who come from the West and from the important province of Ontario where a campaign is in progress having for its object retrenchment and the exercise of care in the expenditure of every dollar of public money. When the minister is putting through this large item of $20,000,000 I observed that the representatives of the West, all along the line, were lustily cheering him and saying in effect: Well done, good and faithful servant, you have thrown the law to the wind, you have constituted yourself the high priest of patronage and you have during the last few years acted regardless of the requirements of the law. I wonder what the careful people and the careful farmers of Ontario and the West who want to know what becomes of their money-and they are right in being cautious and careful in such matters- would say to their representatives here who are almost jumping over their desks in their anxiety to pass this item of $20,000,000 without the slightest attempt to see that we are getting market value for that money. What an enormous amount of eloquence, ingenuity, and physical strength the minister would have conserved if he had simply complied with the law in this matter. When we are endowed with a great deal of ingenuity, eloquence and a capacity to ' get around things we perhaps depend too much upon such qualities. The minister is particularly talented in that direction and I am sorry that he has been put almost to the breaking point and compelled to use to the utmost the ingenuity and talent that he possesses when the very simple process of complying with the law would have avoided the whole of it. In the matter of building the ships there were, I take it, sixty-three separate and distinct contracts; perhaps there were, perhaps there were not; at all events there were sixty-thrse separate and distinct entities, drawing the long bow or going beyond the bounds of ordinary imagination for me to suppose that there were sixty-three different contracts. These contracts, I presume, were ratified by the Government by sixty-three separate Orders in Council.
