Now although the Minister of Marine has raised *this controversy by asking for this appropriation from Parliament he is no more responsible for the passage and the ratification of these contracts than my good friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) who presided over the deliberations of the Cabinet when the Orders in Council

referred to were presented. The President of the Privy Council is a lawyer but the Minister of Marine is not, and the latter in the innocence of his heart perhaps never heard of the provisions of the law which have been quoted to-night until they were brought squarely to his notice by hon. gentlemen on this side. But the President of the Privy Council cannot plead ignorance of the law because he is in the happy position of being a member of the bar.
What bar?
The bar of Ontario, of course.

The President of the Privy Council must have read this law several times and therefore cannot plead ignorance of it. Now, if the Minister of Marine wants to be open and above board with the committee he will table these Orders in Council and show the reasons advanced in those documents upon which the contracts in question were ratified. In doing as he did he was getting away from the law and he must have had to advance sufficient reasons to justify a departure from the statute. Therefore, if the Minister of Marine in respect to the sixty-three contracts which were presented to the learned presiding genius of the Privy Council satisfied his colleagues that his reasons were good, he is no more to blame than the rest of the Cabinet who made a mistake in that connection.
I think my hon. friend the minister (Mr. Ballantyne) could have avoided all these difficulties by having all those Orders in Council brought down and saying: Here are the reasons I gave the Government; those reasons were good enough for the Government, and I am no more responsible for the policy adopted than aie my colleagues. But I rather fear there are no such reasons, and that no business course was followed by him. I am inclined to believe that he had with him an aggregation of gentlemen just as willing to partake of the advantages of this patronage as he was himself-not personally, of course, but we know what are the advantages to a Government of such fat patronage as the millions that have been spent in this connection. I would advise the minister that in future it will be easier for him and for his successors to follow the law and let us have competition in every line of business, rather than constitute himself the dispenser of patronage among a few chosen concerns. It is not business, and I venture to say that he met

hut very few returned soldiers in the emergencies and necessities he imagined.
The hon. minister has not been in this House as long as some of us. During 1910, 1911 and 1912 we were told by his leader- not the acting leader but the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden-that it would take us fifty years to have anything like a decent knowledge of shipbuilding, that we had no men here who could build ships, and that there was not a particle of God's green earth in this country strong enough to hold up a ship. But now we have this changed condition of things, that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries can take sixty ships in his hands, throw them around, and call upon returned soldiers just as they land, and, without the slightest training along these lines, place them in shipyards, and awa'y they go as first-class shipbuilders! What a wonderful transition has taken place, and what a magic wand my hon. friend wields when he can shake it over those fellows and immediately they are transformed into first-class designers, shipbuilders, and riveters,-taken right from the trenches with the mud still on their boots-men who can do anything from the keel to the masthead! These are wonderful days! Let me say again to the minister that he made a great blunder in trying to get away from the law even at the advantage of giving work to the returned soldiers-and so far we have had no evidence that those men received any such benefit.
I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without reminding the minister that there is something else behind this shipbuilding programme which has escaped the notice of himself and of other hon. members around him. I remember, Sir, when I was going to school long ago one of our books contained an article about a boy called "Solomon Slow," who was said to be the son of a gentleman. I have no doubt that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is "the son oi a gentleman" and also more or less of a Solomon Slow. It will be remembered that in 1909 this country adopted a naval and shipbuilding policy. We could have built ships at that stage for .$50 a ton, whereas we are now paying nearly four times that sum. But for political purposes-and this is what I want to bring home to the minister and to the people of this country-the party which sits behind the minister and this Government-because, after all, it is one and the same Government-abandoned the naval policy and abandoned also the shipbuilding policy we then adopted. As any person will see on perusing the speech of the Right

Hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) who spoke on that resolution on the 29th of March, 1909, the very policy now being pursued was then outlined in his speech and in the speech of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier; in fact, everything we are doing- now was contemplated at that time. After hon. gentlemen opposite came into power we did all we could to impress upon them the necessity of getting to work at once and building ships, but year after year went by, the war came, prices went up, and what could have been obtained for $50 a ton at the time we were urging action is now costing them $190 and possibly $200. I think it is only right to bring to the notice of the country that this dilatoriness and the hope of gaining a party advantage by refusing to accept our policy have landed the country in the expensive program which is being carried out to-day.
I wish to pay some slight attention to my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) in reference to the plate mill at Sydney. He finds fault with the building of that mill. I took issue with him on "that point when it was discussed last summer. He says that on account of the attitude I then took I lost the leadership of my party. I would say to my hon. friend that if the two things were put up to me: McKenzie, you are going to lose the leadership; or the [plate mill is going to be built at Sydney, I would say every time: Let me lose the leadership, and let the plate mill be built. I am satisfied, Sir, that the course I took on that oooasion was the proper course, and that the building of the plate mill will be one of the best things that ever happened for this Dominion. Some hon. ' gentlemen,are very much opposed to subsidizing the building of ships. I never had oocasion to consider the question, and therefore I am not going to commit myself i one way or the other.
Hear, hear.
Some hon. gentlemen say ironically "hear, hear." I have been quite a long time in this House and I have never yet hedged on anything.
Oh, oh.

When I had to do a thing I did it right square up. If I have to put myself on record about subsidizing the building of ships, when the occasion arises I shall not have very much hesitation about it one way or the other. But I do say to you, Sir, and to hon. gentlemen, that if the question of subsidies is such a frightful thing, it ought to be equally bad 58
in all respects. I would like to ask hon. gentlemen from the West, and particularly my hon. friend from Red Deer, if he is opposed even to-day to the subsidizing of the building of the Canadian Pacific? Is he opposed to the subsidizing of the building of railways in every part of Canada, particularly in the West? Subsidies are necessary for railways to encourage their building and to' give railway facilities in places where the roads wou'd not otherwise be built. If that is a good thing,-and nobody in this House would contend that the subsidizing o>f railways was a mistake, -what is wrong with subsidizing steel, as we had it done in Sydney, or subsidizing the building of ships, if we cannot get them built otherwise and the progress and development of the country require their building? I see very little, difference between one and the other, and although we have paid hundreds of millions of dollars by way of subsidies for the building of railways throughout this country, I do not think 'any hon. member would take the responsibility of saying that those subsidies should not have been granted.
Now, we have not yet reached the stage of finally passing judgment upon whether or not subsidies for shipbuilding shall he granted, but if the subject should come up I am sure, Sir, it will receive careful and deliberate consideration, and whatever is regarded as in the best interests of the country will be done. I hope that my hon. friend, who has got himself into so much trouble in connection with these contracts, will in the future, in connection with shipbuilding or any contacts that he may have to deal with, himself look up the statutes, even though he is not a lawyer, and not depend for everything, his Shorter catechism and all the lest, upon the uplifting influence of my good friend the President of the Council.
How many of these boats were in service in inland waters during the last season?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None have been placed on inland waters as yet, but now that we are getting from the yards a large number of ships which are of lake size I should think that a good many will be placed on the Great Lakes shortly.

The minister can do nothing better than place as many of these boats on our inland waters as it is possible to place there. So far as transportation is concerned there has been operating in our inland waters the octopus of high rates,



whose tentacles have stretched out to such an extent that we are now paying freight rates three or four hundred per cent higher than we were paying a few years ago. The minister has a splendid field there, a good, profitable field. He may encounter some little opposition; I venture to say that had his programme been primarily intended for the inland waters he might not have received the support that he got a few days ago from some members representing constituencies particularly interested in inland water transportation. However, he may rest assured that he will have strong support from Western Canada if he will undertake to deal with this octopus which has been operating in our inland waters.

I do not wish to delay the passing of this item. The matter is one of considerable importance; it involves the payment by the taxpayers of Canada of several millions of dollars. I- assume that the Minister of Finance will find some way of getting the money, and then the taxpayers will have to pay the bill. However, what I particularly wish to discuss is the statement made by the minister a moment ago that now that we are getting so many of these ships, some of them will be operated in inland waters. For several years there was discussed in this House the advisability of utilizing the great natural waterway of the Ottawa district right up to the head of the Lakes in order to enable Western Canada to ship its grain to Liverpool with only one transshipment, and that at Fort William. That could easily have been done. It would have cost a few millions, but Governments a very few years ago were wary about spending millions even for the purposes of such great utility. The present Government, for reasons best known to' themselves, thought it wiser to expend millions in the building of what is to-day known as the Welland Canal. I am not going to criticize the Government for the building of the Welland Canal. I have always been in favour of extending our water transportation, for it is the cheapest means of enabling our farmers to get their products to the markets of the world. But, Sir, the Welland Canal is becoming a very expensive institution. This year the poor Finance Minister will be called upon to take a few more millions out of the pockets of the ' people to be expended upon that project, and I do not think any member of the Cabinet can tell us when that expenditure will cease. Will the minister make a statement to-night whether in put-

ting his boats on the inland waters he proposes to take such steps as will enable the Western country to send its grain through Fort William to the markets of the world via the Ottawa district waterway system? When I speak of the Ottawa district, I speak of it as extending all the way to Fort William. I do not want to intrude upon what the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) has so ably advocated in the House on numerous occasions, but among the districts served by the utilization of this water route would be the New Ontario section and the Timiskaming section, on the Quebec as well as on the Ontario side, a district abounding in lumber and pulpwood. Will the minister give our mines, the richest in all Canada, a chance to be developed?- and when I say mines, I include the iron ore that is to be found in great quantities within reach of Ottawa. Will he give those who wish to take that iron ore from the ground a chance to ship with only one transshipment? Will be give to the farmers of that great section extending to Fort William a chance to ship conveniently their products out to the markets of the world? Is it the intention of the minister, when placing these boats on inland waters, to place them on one of the greatest waterways that Nature could give to any country?
I speak of the Ottawa waterway known to most members of this House, in its immediate vicinity, known from say Des-chenes right outside of Ottawa city to the Chats Falls, a distance of twenty-five miles, without a perceptible current, without the necessity of putting a lock or a dredge on the river and with a deep channel, perhaps, with a few locks higher up and a few . more higher up still. The West will benefit; the East will benefit, Ontario and Quebec will benefit; my hon. friends from Nova Scotia will benefit, because when the ships come back after they have been unloaded, they will be able to bring to the people of Ontario the coal and steel of Nova Scotia. It is a well known fact that coal cannot very well go past the city of Montreal to-day on account of the high railway rates and on account of its bulkiness making it difficult of transportation by rail. It is, however, the easiest thing in the world and the cheapest way to transport it by water. I know the minister might say to me that the building of such works is dependent upon the Public Works Department; but I ask him on account of the statement he made to-night, if, in connection with the ships that he has built, he will advocate my suggestion with his

colleagues in the Cabinet, with the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), with the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), who has a happy way of finding millions of dollars. Formerly, we were shy when we asked for a few hundred thousand dollars to expend on this system; aye, a million or two was a big amount; but to-day, if a man speaks in the millions, he is hardly understood.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I regret very much
to have to call the hon. member to order, but this is not only a passing reference to the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. He has already admitted that it is not relevant to this item.

I comply with your ruling. I do not know if I mentioned the Georgian Bay canal; I mentioned the Welland canal, and perhaps I was out of order. I know, however, the rules of the House and I do not wish to appeal from your ruling at all. I simply wish to ask the minister to make a statement whether, when he is putting the boats on the inland waters, he will consider placing them on the Ottawa river higher up.
Mr. BALLANTYNE; I shall be very glad to bring the hon. member's proposal to the attention of the management.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I be permitted, as the Minister of Finance is in his seat, to ask him if the Government considers that it is going to be possible to meet this expenditure of $20,000,000 and other proposed expenditures that have been brought down without a further loan, or whether we may expect a loan in the course of the next fiscal year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am very sorry to say to the hon. leader of the Opposition that his question is not in order at the present stage. We are now in Committee of Supply, and it could only be asked in Committee of Ways and Means.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I bow immediately to your ruling Mr. Chairman, nevertheless this question has a very important bearing on Whether or not we should vote such a l-arge amount as $20,000,000. Before we do so, we should know where the money is to come from. It is one thing to vote $20,000,000 out of current revenue, and it is another thing to be asked to vote that sum to be met by a further loan. For my part, I prefer to hold the Estimate until we get from the Minister of Finance a statement in that connection.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I may assure the hon. leader of the Opposition that the money cannot be expended until it has been provided by the Committee of Ways and Means. When the House sits as a Committee of Ways and Means, the hon. member's question will be perfectly in order.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: With all due regard to your ruling, Sir, it is very important that the committee should know where we are to get this money from.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have already decided when the question may be asked and when it must be answered. If the hon. member wishes to appeal from my ruling, he has, of course, an absolute right to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Probably, if you are willing, Sir, the Minister of Finance might make a statement.

Am I to understand that
the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) is to make a statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have ruled three
times that the question is out of order, and I hope the committee will abide by the ruling.
Mr.' POWER: I asked the question simply because I thought the Minister of Finance wished to speak. I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to a question which I put to him this afternoon when the Orders of the Day were called. I drew his attention to the fact that there were four ships belonging to the Canadian Merchant Marine at present lying in the harbour of Quebec, and that cargoes could be provided for them by utilizing the Canadian National railways. We have been told again this-evening that one of the principal reasons for creating our merchant marine was that it should work in conjunction with the Canadian National railways. There are, however, four ships now lying in the harbour of Quebec; the river is open; the port authorities at Quebec, the Board of Trade, have, I understand, requested the minister to' load these ships and to send them to sea; and when I asked a question in reference to this matter this afternoon, I was told that that the minister had nothing whatsoever to do with the matter, and I was referred ito the management of the Canadian Mercantile Marine. Surely, the minister who gives us a report as to its profits and loss in a year's operations, should be interested in knowing whether or not his hirelings, his employees, are conducting the affairs of this mercantile marine properly. It must cost some money

for ships like those lying in the harbour of Quebec to remain there for some time when cargoes could easily be obtained. Why does the minister not inquire from his officials, from those under his jurisdiction, or rather under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Railways and Canals? I may say in passing that before we opened this discussion, I had thought of asking this question, and that is why I asked the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. J. D. Reid) to remain in the House. Some hon. gentlemen thought it was a joke when I requested him to remain here and that I was trying to be satirical and ironical when I referred to the valuable contribution he had made to the debates last Tuesday. I had no such intention; I simply wanted the Minister of Railways to tell us why he permitted ships to remain in harbour when they might obtain cargoes. Since he is not here, I shall have to ask the Minister of Marine to give me some information with regard to the matter. '

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The answer is a
very simple one. Those ships were not ready to go to sea before the ice formed so thick that it would be impossible to send them to sea. There is a second reason. All the ships at Quebec at the present time are having tween-decks put in them.
Was not this work performed during the winter? In the past considerable work of that nature has been done at the port of Quebec, and elsewhere, I suppose.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This work has been carried on during the winter.
Then why are not the ships ready for navigation in the spring?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They will be ready when navigation is. open.
Navigation is open now.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am sorry I must differ with my hon. friend.

A boat, The Labrador, left Quebec not ten days ago for the north shore and back. It went as far down the river as there was any likelihood of meeting serious trouble from ice or from the climatic conditions at this season of the year. In other years boats have left for Gulf ports during the months of January and February. I find that boats have left for the Gulf ports on March 16, 23, 24, 26 and 31. A boat left on March 28 for the Gulf ports one year and returned on April 6, so there is no great exaggeration in my statement that navigation is open. In any

case, if navigation were not open at this very moment, it seems to me it would be the duty of this Government and of the company which undertakes the operation of these boats to have a cargo ready for them. The minister will surely not suggest that navigation will" not be open from the port of Quebec to the sea long before it is open from the port of Montreal to the sea. So I think it would be well to arrange for cargoes at Quebec in order to utilize these boats. I think the minister ought to give some other explanation than the one he has given. I do not think it will be satisfactory to the seafaring people of my constituency and of the district of Quebec, who know something about climatic and navigation conditions at this time of the year. I think the minister owes it to his own reputation, to the port of Quebec and to the country, to see that proper precautions are taken to see that these boats are not laid up a long time, and that the best possible service is given by the boats under the control of himself and his colleague.
Have any contracts for ships been given out sir^ce the first of October last?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
How many?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Seven or eight contracts have been actually signed since then, but they were agreed upon considerably prior to October.

Were there any
contracts agreed upon after the first of October?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Two ships with the Coughlan Shipbuilding Company of Vancouver, and two with the Wallace Shipbuilding Company. The reason for the long delay in signing contracts with both companies was because of a difference of opinion as to price, owing' to a change in the ships from coal-burning to oil-burning.
Do I understand the minister to state that a contract was agreed upon after the first of October?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know the exact date, but I should say, yes.

Mr. Chairman, I think we have here a clear example of the danger of letting contracts without tender. In the month of September last I had an interview with a high official of the Department of Marine, and I inquired from him whether the Government was going to let

any more contracts for ships. Some clients of mine from British Columbia had asked me to get this information. I was assnrred then by this high official that no more contracts would be let. That was in the month of September last. Now we have the admission of the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: May I ask a question? There are only two steel shipbuilding companies in Vancouver, and contracts have been placed with both of them. Will the hon. member give me the name of the firm he represents?

Never mind the
name now. I do not. think any hon. member will doubt the truth of my statement. I repeat, I had an interview with a high official of the Department of Marine regarding contracts for ships, and his statement was that the Government programme was completely filled, and that there would be no more contracts let. That was in the month of September last. Now we have the admission of the minister that there were four contracts given for ships after the first of jOctober. I submit that was a clear case of patronage. I submit that it is a very dangerous thing to depart from the law which compels the calling for tenders for any item over $5,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When I asked the question a moment ago, I was endeavouring to facilitate the passing of this item, and unless means can be found whereby the Government can state its position in the matter of a further loan to-night, I would ask the minister to allow the committee to rise and report progress-it is about midnight-so as to give the Government a chance to bring down a statement.
, Some hon. MEMBERS: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I might make our position perfectly clear so far as we on this side of the House are concerned. We believe that the people of this country are not prepared to vote millions of dollars as a result of only a few hours' discussion, iwithout knowing where the money is to come 'from to meet those expenditures. We believe the people of this country will want to know whether these expenditures will be met out of the revenues the Government believes it is going to be possible for it to get in the regular way, or whether they are to be met out of further loans. That reaches the very foundation of the Estimates the Government is going to bring down. I might as well infoim my hon. friends opposite that we on this side of the House
will continue to press for a knowledge of the Government's position on that matter. I certainly do not feel like voting $20,000,000 foi the purpose that is suggested here tonight, until I know whether the Government is going to demand a further loan out of which to meet the expenditure. I feel in exactly the same position in regard to most of the othei items that have been brought down in the Estimates. So I say to the Government, they will facilitate the business of Parliament if they make a statement on this point at the earliest possible moment, for until they do I should not. like to see another item carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must surely know that the methods of raising money that the Government proposes to adopt are not disclosed until the Budget is brought down, and it is entirely imprqper and irregular to make any reference to Budget proposals before that occasion. Further than that, we cannot go. I am perfectly willing, however, to tell my hon. friend that at the moment I certainly have no idea of another popular loan.

The Minister of Finance has just made a statement which wmuld have been sound and would have held sway in this House some fifteen or twenty years ago. But to-day the people of Canada are not so much concerned about formality and the technicalities of the rules of this House in the consideration of the taxes which they have to pay. My hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition, in the stand which he has taken has simply stated that we on this side of the House, who claim to have some responsibility to the public-and hon. gentlemen on the other side will readily agree with me that we have some responsibility, because we do represent some of the taxpayers of Canada-are not in favour of the practice, which seems to have been in vogue during the last few years, of having expenditures of millions of dollars foisted upon the Canadian people by a system of Orders in Council or by the mere statement of a minister who gets up and says: I assure you it is all right, and we need the money. I say with all deference to my hon. friend, the Minister of Naval Service (Mr. Ballantyne), that I for one should not like to be a judge of any man on either side of this House. I should not like to be charged with the keeping of any other conscience than my own; but I do say that it will facilitate and shorten the labour of the session, and help the work of ministers, if they would give all the information sought by

the people through the requests made by the Opposition. If they would do this they would find that it would be cheaper in the long run. I readily agree with what the Minister of Finance has said, that it is usual to wait for the Budget speech for a statement as to the country's finances and how public needs are to be met. But, Mr. Chairman, the minister will readily understand that when it comes to consideration of an item which carries with it the expenditure of millions of dollars, neither he nor I, nor any of the taxpayers of Canada who will be called upon to pay this sum of money, will be satisfied with a simple statement that the time to give information as to whether we shall meet this money by a loan or otherwise, will be given in the Budget speech.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I must ask my hon. friends to accept the ruling of the Chair. My hon. friends know perfectly well that the ruling .which the chairman has given is but the statement of the invariable practice of the House. What my hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) is suggesting at the close of the day, when it was understood the item would be disposed of-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There was no such understanding.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
At the end of the day my hon. friend raises a question which he knows is contrary to the whole practice and procedure of Parliament since Confederation. Supply has never been held up pending the bringing down of Budget proposals, and there can be no new statement by the Minister of Finance as to general sources of revenue until the Budget is brought down. If my hon. friend wishes to take the responsibility of seeking to overturn the whole parliamentary procedure and practice in connection with the voting of Supply he is quite entitled to do so, but he cannot rise and say that so far as he is concerned the business of the House will be held up on that account, or intimidate the Government by any such statement. The Government is anxious to proceed. For two days full information has been given on the item, and all questions have been answered and now my hon. friend says that unless the Minister of Finance will rise and outline the financial proposals of the Government in reference to the raising of revenue, then the Opposition will hold up this item. The position, I say wth great respect to my hon. friend' is wholly unwarranted and unprecedented. The Government could not

possibly accede to any such proposal as he has suggested, that the Budget speech should be anticipated on a question like this in Supply. All I ask my hon. friends to do is to recognize the ruling of the Chairman, who has but stated the invariable parliamentary practice in this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I desire to say that I have given frankly and fully every bit of information which it was humanly possible for me to give to hon. members. I could not have given it more fully if the members were ordinary shareholders in any large corporation. I appreciate very much the attitude of the leader of the Opposition and hon. members on the other side. They were quite within their rights in asking the questions they asked, and I am only too glad to have been given an opportunity to answer them as fully as I did. Now that that has all been done. I hope the leader of the Opposition and those associated with him will allow the item to pass.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I should wish to be the last to delay the proceedings, and, as I said a moment ago, I had in view only the facilitating of the passage of this item. The President of the Privy Council is entirely unwarranted in the statement that I am trying to change the procedure and practice of this House. It is no fault of the Opposition that we are now at the Easter recess and the Budget has not been brought down. I will point out to my hon friend that since Confederation there has been an understanding, in regard to the voting of Supply, that the revenues would be raised in the regular way. The irregular practice of the financing of loans was not a consideration formerly; to-day it is the biggest consideration in this country. I contend that there is no question in which the- people of Canada are as vitally interested as the question of public expenditure and the taxation that may be necessary to meet it. It is quite impossible for us on this side of the House, who recognize the obligation we have to the people of the country, to be indifferent to the question whether or not further loans are to be raised in Canada to meet public expenditures, and what particular taxation the Government intends to resort to. To give point to what I say, let me repeat that I think it would be well for the minister to bring down the (Budget at a very early date and, before proceeding much further with the Estimates, to inform the House how soon we may expect it. Because I may tell my hon. friends opposite

-not in any spirit of intimidation, but solely for the purpose of safeguarding the interests of the Canadian public-that the stand that we intend to take on this side ot the House with regard to public expenditures will depend very much upon the nature of the Budget which is presented.
I am glad the Chairman raised the point he did because it will enable us-and perhaps will enable the Government also- to see where we stand in the matter of further discussions on the Estimates. I cannot make it too plain that, until we get some intimation from the Government as to how it purposes to raise the revenues, it will be difficult for us to say whether particular items shall or shall not pass.
'Mr. JACOBS: Before the item passes 1 wish to say that I am much disturbed in my mind as to the position in which the Minister of Marine finds himself owing to the fact that these contracts have been let without tender. If I remember well when the matter first came up the minister told the House that the contracts were of such a nature that it was impossible-having regard to the business of the country and the business of the department-to have tenders called for, that the nature of the business did not permit of the calling for tenders. Now, as I understand it, to-night the minister has changed his view. He says that an emergency existed and that consequently the rule requiring the calling for tenders had to be suspended and done away with. I do not agree with him, Mr. Chairman, and I wish to Tecord my protest against the action of a responsible minister of the Crown in ignoring the solemn text of the law as its exists in this case. . If the ministers of the Crown, if the keepers of the King's conscience, do not obey the law, how can you expect the rank and file to do so? Never was there a clearer case made out against the Government and a minister thfm has been made out here, and it seems to me that some action ought to be taken by this House and by the Government to protect the' minister against proceedings which may be brought against him-probably in the nature of impeachment, or otherwise; I am not here to suggest what the proceedings should be or what the minister has laid himself open to. But it does seem to me that when a Minister of the Crown wilfully disobeys the law in the manner in which the Minister of Marine has done, surely the arm of, the law is long enough to reach that minister.
What I particularly object to to-night is the fact that the minister should have shifted his ground. We went away last week comfortably believing that the minister in his wisdom was right when he said that the nature of the business did not permit of the calling for tenders. He explained why and gave us the details. Why is it that the minister has now changed his view? I think it ought to be made clear to him that in matters of this kind the law ought to be followed, and that for every ship there should be a tender.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In view of the statement which the Minister of Finance has made that at the present time he does not contemplate another loan, so far as I am concerned I am quite prepared that this particular item should pass, but I wish again to repeat what I have already said, that the sooner the Government can see its way to bring down the Budget, the better it will be for expedition of business in many directions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No.
Some hon. MEMBER'S: Yes

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In my opinion yeas have it. I declare the item carried.
Progress reported. '
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Ballantyne the House adjourned at 12.10 a.m. Wednesday.
Wednesday, March 31, 1920.
